Abstract

Unlike the classical Heston model, Fourier pricing under the rough Heston model requires solving a fractional Riccati equation at every quadrature point. Since the required resolution varies with model parameters and quadrature point, a single uniform time discretization can be inefficient. We develop single- and multilevel Gauss-Laguerre quadrature methods that balance the time discretization and Fourier quadrature errors. Both methods scale the laguerre weight to the estimated Fourier integrand decay. The single-level method allocates a prescribed tolerance between the two errors. The multilevel method splits the integrand into a level-zero term and level differences, selecting quadrature points separately at each level. Suppose that the Fourier integrand discretization error is 𝒪⁡(Δ​tp)\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^{p}), that evaluating the characteristic function once costs 𝒪⁡(Δ​t−β)\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^{-\beta}), and that the algebraic Gauss-Laguerre quadrature error is 𝒪(N−sSL/2)\mathcal{O}(N^{-s_{\mathrm{SL}}/2}), where sSLs_{\mathrm{SL}} is the smoothness index. Under this estimate and assumptions on the regularity and decay of level differences, we prove that the proposed single-level method requires 𝒪⁡(ε−(β/p+2/sSL))\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-(\beta/p+2/s_{\mathrm{SL}})}) computational work to achieve accuracy ε\varepsilon, whereas the proposed multilevel method requires 𝒪(ε−β/p)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-\beta/p}) computational work. We also study root-exponential Gauss-Laguerre error models for practical multilevel quadrature allocation. Numerical experiments support the observed fractional Riccati and Fourier integrand convergence rates and root-exponential quadrature behavior, and show substantial reductions in quadrature cost from the proposed scaling. The multilevel method provides clear computational savings over the single-level method. We further benchmark the multilevel fractional Riccati method against the BL2 Markovian approximation [7] and report lower total CPU time in the tested configurations.

1 Introduction

Fourier methods [30, 15, 21] form the basis of many of the most efficient pricing and calibration routines used in Markovian stochastic volatility [22], jump-diffusion [17], and Lévy models [34]. This efficiency stems from the availability of the characteristic function of the log price process, which allows option valuation problems to be recast as Fourier inversion problems, replacing stochastic simulation-based methods by the numerical evaluation of deterministic contour integrals of analytic, but possibly oscillatory, functions in the Fourier domain [33].

In Markovian affine stochastic volatility models, the characteristic function is available in closed form as the explicit solution of systems of generalized Riccati ordinary differential equations (ODEs) [17]. A canonical example is the Heston model [28], which remains widely used in equity and foreign exchange markets [22]. However, empirical evidence [10] has revealed systematic shortcomings of such models in reproducing the behavior of implied volatility surfaces, in particular the pronounced steepness of the at-the-money skew at short maturities [9]. These observations motivated the development of rough volatility models, which incorporate memory effects by modeling the driving noise of the volatility process as a fractional Brownian motion. Prominent examples include the rough Bergomi model [9] and the rough Heston model [19].

The loss of Markovianity precludes the direct application of classical partial differential equation (PDE)-based pricing techniques and increases the computational complexity of Monte Carlo simulation methods due to the path-dependent nature of the volatility dynamics [8, 9]. Despite these challenges, Fourier-based pricing methods remain attractive in the rough Heston setting, following the seminal work of [20], who showed that the characteristic function admits a semi-explicit exponential-affine representation. As a consequence, option pricing can be reformulated as the numerical evaluation of a deterministic Fourier integral; however, in contrast to the Markovian affine case, this requires solving a fractional Riccati equation independently at each quadrature point, which becomes a major computational bottleneck in calibration settings where the characteristic function must be evaluated repeatedly across many parameter values.

This computational challenge has motivated two complementary lines of research aimed at restoring numerical tractability while preserving the features of rough volatility dynamics. A first line of work replaces the original non-Markovian volatility process by a Markovian surrogate, constructed by approximating the fractional kernel by a finite sum of exponentials [1, 2, 7]. The exponential terms introduce a collection of mean-reverting factors and yield a finite-dimensional Markovian representation. The resulting model retains the ability to reproduce key empirical features of rough volatility while replacing the fractional Riccati equation governing the characteristic function by a finite-dimensional system of classical Riccati ODEs.

A second line of research retains the original rough volatility model and instead seeks to accelerate valuation directly. A substantial body of work within this line focuses on improving the numerical solution of the fractional Riccati equation itself. The standard approach remains the fractional Adams predictor-corrector scheme [16], which has been widely adopted in the rough volatility literature. Its direct implementation evaluates a discrete convolution over the full history at each time step and therefore requires 𝒪⁡(Δ​t−2)\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^{-2}) operations over a fixed time interval [31, 14]. Several refinements have been proposed to enhance its efficiency, including Richardson-Romberg extrapolation combined with fractional power series expansions [14], rational approximation techniques that construct fast surrogates for the Riccati solution [23], as well as modified Adams-type schemes with improved stability and performance properties [12]. In parallel, other works have sought to accelerate Fourier pricing by focusing on the numerical evaluation of the Fourier integral itself, for instance through contour deformations and SINH-type accelerations [12], or by adopting alternative transform-based methodologies such as the SINC method [5]. These approaches improve the numerical resolution of the fractional Riccati solver or the efficiency of the quadrature, but treat the two components largely in isolation.

Despite this progress, several theoretical and numerical issues remain only partially understood and continue to constrain robust and systematically optimized implementations. First, a full characterization of the relevant strip of analyticity of the rough Heston characteristic function is not available in explicit form, complicating principled contour selection and the tuning of damping parameters [12, 6]. In this work, we propose a practical heuristic that extends the guideline for contour selection of [6] to settings in which the analyticity strip is not available in closed form. Second, in contrast to the classical Heston model, for which the asymptotic behaviour of the characteristic function for large values of the Fourier integration variable is available in explicit form [3], no comparably rigorous asymptotic characterization has been derived for the rough Heston model. This gap complicates the construction of quadrature rules adapted to the tail behaviour and integral transformations, including the domain transformation strategies for quasi-Monte Carlo [11] and the double exponential quadrature method proposed in [4].

The present work follows the second line of research in that it retains the exact rough Heston model and its fractional Riccati representation. Rather than studying the fractional Riccati solver and the Fourier quadrature separately, we control their errors jointly and allocate the work required to meet a prescribed tolerance optimally. A related work derives an allocation of computational work between numerical quadrature and optimization that minimizes the cost of computing multivariate shortfall risk measures [26]. While the time step determines the accuracy and cost of each characteristic function evaluation, the quadrature error estimate allows us to determine the number of required quadrature points in the Fourier domain. We first propose a single-level method that allocates the tolerance between the time discretization and quadrature errors and uses a scaled Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule whose weight is matched to the estimated decay of the Fourier integrand to prevent issues documented for short maturities in [12]. We then extend the construction to a multilevel method, which applies the scaled Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule to a level zero term and a hierarchy of level differences. This construction follows the deterministic telescoping-quadrature paradigm [27, 25]; its specific contribution here is to apply the hierarchy jointly to the Fourier quadrature and the fractional-Riccati time discretization. The proposed multilevel method selects the number of quadrature points separately at each level to optimally distribute the work over the hierarchy. Our main contributions are as follows.

  • •

    We develop a single-level Fourier pricing method based on scaled Gauss-Laguerre quadrature. The pricing error is decomposed into a fractional-Riccati time-discretization error and a Fourier quadrature error, and the prescribed tolerance is allocated between them. The Laguerre scaling is chosen to reflect the decay of the Fourier integrand, and both algebraic and root-exponential quadrature error models are analyzed.

  • •

    Let pp denote the convergence order of the Fourier integrand under refinement of the fractional- Riccati time discretization, β\beta the per-node cost exponent, and sSLs_{\mathrm{SL}} the algebraic Gauss- Laguerre convergence exponent of the single-level integrand. We show that balancing the time-discretization and quadrature errors gives

    WSL(ε)=𝒪(ε−β/p−2/sSL).W_{\mathrm{SL}}(\varepsilon)=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\varepsilon^{-\beta/p-2/s_{\mathrm{SL}}}\right).

    We then develop a multilevel method based on a telescopic decomposition of the discretized Fourier integrand and level-dependent quadrature allocation. By exploiting the decay of the multilevel corrections, the method achieves

    WML(ε)=𝒪(ε−β/p)W_{\mathrm{ML}}(\varepsilon)=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\varepsilon^{-\beta/p}\right)

    under the stated algebraic regularity and correction-decay assumptions. Root-exponential quadrature models are additionally used for the practical multilevel allocation.

  • •

    Numerical experiments support the observed fractional-Riccati/Fourier-integrand convergence rates and root-exponential quadrature behavior, and demonstrate substantial reductions in quadrature cost from the proposed scaling. We compare the single- and multilevel methods in terms of computational work and CPU time and observe clear savings from the multilevel construction. Finally, we benchmark the multilevel direct fractional-Riccati method against the BL2 Markovian approximation [7] and report lower total CPU time in the four tested configurations, subject to reference-assisted BL2 factor selection.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the pricing framework and the Fourier representation. Section 3 develops the single- and multilevel methods and establishes their error and complexity estimates. Section 4 tests these estimates, examines the effects of scaling the Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule and allocating quadrature points among the levels, and presents the comparison with the BL2 benchmark. Finally, Section 5 concludes and discusses possible extensions.

2 Problem Setting and Pricing Framework

In this section, we formulate the valuation problem in Fourier space, state the underlying assumptions on the model and the payoff function, and fix the notation used throughout the paper. Section 2.1 introduces the Fourier pricing representation and the associated notation, while Section 2.2 specifies the rough Heston dynamics and the payoff considered in this work.

A general treatment of admissibility conditions for Fourier pricing formulas, covering different regularity and integrability assumptions on the payoff and the characteristic function, is given in [18]. In the rough Heston model, however, the admissible strip of analyticity of the characteristic function is not known explicitly, in contrast to many Lévy models. This complicates the selection of the damping parameter. We therefore propose, in Section 4, a practical selection rule that extends the approach of [6]. Alternative choices of the damping parameter and the integration contour are discussed, for example, in [12].

2.2 Payoff and Asset Model

In this section, we specify the payoff of interest and introduce the underlying asset model used throughout this work.

2.2.1 Payoff and its Fourier Transform

Although the proposed framework can be extended to a wide variety of payoff functions (see [18]), in this work we focus the European call option. Its payoff, for K>0K>0, is defined by

P⁡(XT)=max⁡(eXT−K, 0).P(X_{T})=\max(e^{X_{T}}-K,\,0). (4)

The corresponding Fourier transform of the payoff function is given by

P^​(ξ)=−K 1−i​ξξ2+i​ξ,\widehat{P}(\xi)=-\,\frac{K^{\,1-\mathrm{i}\xi}}{\xi^{2}+\mathrm{i}\xi}, (5)

where ξ:=u+i​R\xi:=u+\mathrm{i}R with u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R} and R∈δP={R∈ℝ∣R<−1}.R\in\delta_{P}=\bigl\{R\in\mathbb{R}\mid R<-1\bigr\}.

ϕ⁡(ξ,t)=exp⁡(i​ξ​(X0+r​t)+∫0t[θ​γ​h​(ξ,s)+V0​F​(ξ,h⁡(ξ,s))]​𝑑s),0≤t≤T.\phi(\xi,t)=\exp\!\left(\mathrm{i}\xi\bigl(X_{0}+rt\bigr)+\int_{0}^{t}\left[\theta\gamma h(\xi,s)+V_{0}F\!\bigl(\xi,h(\xi,s)\bigr)\right]\,ds\right),\hskip 18.49988pt0\leq t\leq T.

This representation avoids a separate numerical approximation of the fractional integral It1−α​h​(ξ,t){I_{t}^{1-\alpha}}h(\xi,t). Since the Fourier pricing formula in Proposition 1 uses the characteristic function at maturity TT, we write

Φ⁡(ξ):=ϕ⁡(ξ,T)=exp⁡(G⁡(ξ)),\Phi(\xi):=\phi(\xi,T)=\exp\!\bigl(G(\xi)\bigr),

where the characteristic function exponent is given by

G⁡(ξ):=i​ξ​(X0+r​T)+∫0T[θ​γ​h​(ξ,s)+V0​F​(ξ,h⁡(ξ,s))]​𝑑s.G(\xi):=\mathrm{i}\xi\bigl(X_{0}+rT\bigr)+\int_{0}^{T}\left[\theta\gamma h(\xi,s)+V_{0}F\!\bigl(\xi,h(\xi,s)\bigr)\right]\,ds. (10)

3 Methodology and Numerical Analysis

This section develops and analyses single-level and multilevel Gauss-Laguerre quadrature approximations for Fourier pricing under the rough Heston model. At each quadrature point, the characteristic function is evaluated by numerically solving the Riccati-Volterra equation (9).

3.1 Discretization of the Fractional Riccati Equation

Let Δ​t0>0\Delta t_{0}>0 and define the hierarchy Δ​tℓ:=2−ℓ​Δ​t0\Delta t_{\ell}:=2^{-\ell}\Delta t_{0}, ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0. The coarsest time step Δ​t0\Delta t_{0} is fixed and assumed to be sufficiently small that the discrete Riccati solutions are well defined and numerically stable on the relevant Fourier contour, and that the nodal and time-integration error estimates introduced below hold from level zero onward. Thus, the hierarchy considered in the analysis starts in the asymptotic convergence regime. In the numerical implementation, Δ​t0\Delta t_{0} is treated as a tuning parameter subject to the stability/refinement diagnostic stated below. Developing an automatic cost-aware selection procedure is left for future work. We assume that Mℓ:=T/Δ​tℓM_{\ell}:=T/\Delta t_{\ell} is an integer and set tℓ,j:=j​Δ​tℓt_{\ell,j}:=j\Delta t_{\ell}, j=0,…,Mℓj=0,\ldots,M_{\ell}. The numerical solver returns the nodal values

hℓ,j(ξ):=hℓ(ξ,tℓ,j),j=0,…,Mℓ,h_{\ell,j}(\xi):=h_{\ell}(\xi,t_{\ell,j}),\hskip 18.49988ptj=0,\ldots,M_{\ell},

with hℓ,0​(ξ)=0h_{\ell,0}(\xi)=0. For a grid vector 𝐯=(v0,…,vMℓ)\mathbf{v}=(v_{0},\ldots,v_{M_{\ell}}), define the composite trapezoidal functional

𝒯ℓ​[𝐯]:=Δ​tℓ​(12​v0+∑j=1Mℓ−1vj+12​vMℓ).\mathcal{T}_{\ell}[\mathbf{v}]:=\Delta t_{\ell}\left(\frac{1}{2}v_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{M_{\ell}-1}v_{j}+\frac{1}{2}v_{M_{\ell}}\right). (11)

We also introduce

J⁡(ξ,z):=θ​γ​z+V0​F​(ξ,z).J(\xi,z):=\theta\gamma z+V_{0}F(\xi,z). (12)

The exponent used in all computations is the fully discrete quantity

Gℓ​(ξ)\displaystyle G_{\ell}(\xi) :=i​ξ​(X0+r​T)+𝒯ℓ​[(J⁡(ξ,hℓ,j​(ξ)))j=0Mℓ]\displaystyle:=\mathrm{i}\xi(X_{0}+rT)+\mathcal{T}_{\ell}\left[\left(J\!\left(\xi,h_{\ell,j}(\xi)\right)\right)_{j=0}^{M_{\ell}}\right] (13)
=i​ξ​(X0+r​T)+Δ​tℓ​[12​J​(ξ,hℓ,0​(ξ))+∑j=1Mℓ−1J⁡(ξ,hℓ,j​(ξ))+12​J​(ξ,hℓ,Mℓ​(ξ))].\displaystyle=\mathrm{i}\xi(X_{0}+rT)+\Delta t_{\ell}\left[\frac{1}{2}J\!\left(\xi,h_{\ell,0}(\xi)\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{M_{\ell}-1}J\!\left(\xi,h_{\ell,j}(\xi)\right)+\frac{1}{2}J\!\left(\xi,h_{\ell,M_{\ell}}(\xi)\right)\right].

Thus, unlike the continuous exponent GG in (10), GℓG_{\ell} includes both the nodal Riccati approximation and the numerical integration in time. The corresponding implemented characteristic function is Φℓ​(ξ):=exp⁡(Gℓ​(ξ))\Phi_{\ell}(\xi):=\exp(G_{\ell}(\xi)), and gℓg_{\ell} denotes the Fourier integrand obtained by replacing Φ\Phi with Φℓ\Phi_{\ell} in (2), for u≥0u\geq 0.

The global integrability and quadrature-regularity conditions used below are hypotheses of the analysis; we do not prove that the fully discrete fractional-Adams characteristic function has the required large-frequency decay on the entire Fourier half-line.

Motivated by [31], we assume the following nodal weighted error estimate with a generic convergence order q>0q>0. This allows us to apply the same analysis to any solver satisfying Assumption 3.

Assumption 3 (Nodal Riccati discretization error).

Fix R∈δVR\in\delta_{V}. For each ξ=u+i​R\xi=u+\mathrm{i}R, with u≥0u\geq 0, there exists a constant Cξ>0C_{\xi}>0, independent of ℓ\ell, such that, for every ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0,

|hℓ,j(ξ)−h(ξ,tℓ,j)|≤Cξtℓ,jα−1Δtℓq,j=1,…,Mℓ.\left|h_{\ell,j}(\xi)-h(\xi,t_{\ell,j})\right|\leq C_{\xi}t_{\ell,j}^{\alpha-1}\Delta t_{\ell}^{\,q},\hskip 18.49988ptj=1,\ldots,M_{\ell}. (14)
Assumption 4 (Finite-horizon boundedness of the Riccati solution).

Fix R∈δVR\in\delta_{V}. For each ξ=u+i​R\xi=u+\mathrm{i}R, with u≥0u\geq 0, the fractional Riccati solution exists on [0,T][0,T] and satisfies

h⁡(ξ,⋅)∈C⁡([0,T],ℂ).h(\xi,\cdot)\in C([0,T];\mathbb{C}).

In particular, ‖h⁡(ξ,⋅)‖L∞​(0,T)<∞\|h(\xi,\cdot)\|_{L^{\infty}(0,T)}<\infty.

We next account for the numerical integration in time used in the fully discrete exponent GℓG_{\ell}. For fixed ξ\xi, define

𝒥ξ​(t):=J⁡(ξ,h⁡(ξ,t)),0≤t≤T.\mathcal{J}_{\xi}(t):=J\!\left(\xi,h(\xi,t)\right),\hskip 18.49988pt0\leq t\leq T. (15)
Assumption 5 (Time-integration error in the characteristic function exponent).

Fix R∈δVR\in\delta_{V}. There exists an order rT>0r_{T}>0 such that, for each ξ=u+i​R\xi=u+\mathrm{i}R, with u≥0u\geq 0, there exists a constant Ctime,ξ>0C_{\mathrm{time},\xi}>0, independent of ℓ\ell, satisfying, for every ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0,

|∫0T𝒥ξ​(t)​𝑑t−𝒯ℓ​[(𝒥ξ​(tℓ,j))j=0Mℓ]|≤Ctime,ξ​Δ​tℓrT.\left|\int_{0}^{T}\mathcal{J}_{\xi}(t)\,dt-\mathcal{T}_{\ell}\left[\left(\mathcal{J}_{\xi}(t_{\ell,j})\right)_{j=0}^{M_{\ell}}\right]\right|\leq C_{\mathrm{time},\xi}\Delta t_{\ell}^{\,r_{T}}. (16)

We now study how the nodal Riccati error and the time-integration error propagate to the approximation errors of the characteristic function and the Fourier integrand. Define

Eℓ​(ξ):=G⁡(ξ)−Gℓ​(ξ),pG:=min⁡{q,rT}.E_{\ell}(\xi):=G(\xi)-G_{\ell}(\xi),\hskip 18.49988ptp_{G}:=\min\{q,r_{T}\}. (17)

For u≥0u\geq 0, let

AE​(u):=supℓ≥0Δ​tℓ−pG​|Eℓ​(u+i​R)|.A_{E}(u):=\sup_{\ell\geq 0}\Delta t_{\ell}^{-p_{G}}\left|E_{\ell}(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right|.
Lemma 1 (Discretization error in the characteristic function exponent).

Assume that δV=δX∩δP≠∅\delta_{V}=\delta_{X}\cap\delta_{P}\neq\emptyset and fix R∈δVR\in\delta_{V}. Suppose that Assumptions 3, 4, and 5 hold. Then AE​(u)<∞A_{E}(u)<\infty for every u≥0u\geq 0, and

|Eℓ​(u+i​R)|≤AE​(u)​Δ​tℓpG,u≥0,ℓ≥0.\left|E_{\ell}(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right|\leq A_{E}(u)\Delta t_{\ell}^{\,p_{G}},\hskip 18.49988ptu\geq 0,\hskip 9.24994pt\ell\geq 0. (18)
Proof.

The proof for Lemma 1 is presented in Appendix A. ∎

For the subsequent single-level and multilevel analyses, the relevant discretization rate is the L1L^{1} convergence rate of the Fourier integrand. We denote this rate by p>0p>0.

Assumption 6 (L1L^{1} discretization error of the Fourier integrand).

There exists a constant Cg>0C_{g}>0, independent of ℓ\ell, such that, for sufficiently small Δ​tℓ\Delta t_{\ell},

‖g−gℓ‖L1​(0,∞)≤Cg​Δ​tℓp.\left\|g-g_{\ell}\right\|_{L^{1}(0,\infty)}\leq C_{g}\Delta t_{\ell}^{\,p}. (19)

We next give sufficient conditions under which Assumption 6 holds with p=pGp={\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{G}}. The estimate (18) is pointwise in the Fourier integration variable. For u≥0u\geq 0, define

Ψ⁡(u):=supℓ≥0Δ​tℓ−pG​|1−exp⁡(−Eℓ​(u+i​R))|.\Psi(u):=\sup_{\ell\geq 0}\Delta t_{\ell}^{-{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{G}}}\left|1-\exp\!\left(-E_{\ell}(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right)\right|.

Since Eℓ=G−GℓE_{\ell}=G-G_{\ell} and Φℓ=Φ​exp⁡(−Eℓ)\Phi_{\ell}=\Phi\exp(-E_{\ell}), we introduce the domination function

𝒟R​(u)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{R}(u) :=|P^​(u+i​R)|​|Φ⁡(u+i​R)|​Ψ​(u)\displaystyle:=\left|\widehat{P}(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right|\left|\Phi(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right|\Psi(u) (20)
=supℓ≥0Δ​tℓ−pG​|P^​(u+i​R)|​|Φ⁡(u+i​R)−Φℓ​(u+i​R)|.\displaystyle=\sup_{\ell\geq 0}\Delta t_{\ell}^{-{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{G}}}\left|\widehat{P}(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right|\left|\Phi(u+\mathrm{i}R)-\Phi_{\ell}(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right|.
Conjecture 1 (Integrability of the domination function).

For the fixed damping parameter R∈δVR\in\delta_{V}, the function 𝒟R\mathcal{D}_{R} defined in (20) satisfies 𝒟R∈L1​(0,∞)\mathcal{D}_{R}\in L^{1}(0,\infty).

The role of Conjecture 1 is immediate from the definition of 𝒟R\mathcal{D}_{R}. For every u≥0u\geq 0 and ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0,

|g​(u)−gℓ​(u)|\displaystyle|g(u)-g_{\ell}(u)| ≤e−r​T2​π​|P^​(u+i​R)|​|Φ⁡(u+i​R)−Φℓ​(u+i​R)|\displaystyle\leq\frac{e^{-rT}}{2\pi}\left|\widehat{P}(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right|\left|\Phi(u+\mathrm{i}R)-\Phi_{\ell}(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right| (21)
≤e−r​T2​π​Δ​tℓpG​𝒟R​(u).\displaystyle\leq\frac{e^{-rT}}{2\pi}\Delta t_{\ell}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{G}}}\mathcal{D}_{R}(u).

Thus, the conjectured integrability of 𝒟R\mathcal{D}_{R} is precisely the condition that permits integration of the pointwise characteristic-function error over the Fourier variable. Numerical evidence is provided in Appendix H, using the observed rate pG,obs=1+α{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{G,\mathrm{obs}}=1+\alpha} reported in Section 4.1.

Assumptions 3, 4, and 5, together with Conjecture 1 yield the following estimate.

Proposition 2 (L1L^{1} discretization error of the Fourier integrand).

Suppose that Assumptions 3, 4, and 5, and Conjecture 1 hold. Then there exists a constant Cg>0C_{g}>0, independent of ℓ\ell, such that

‖g−gℓ‖L1​(0,∞)≤Cg​Δ​tℓpG,ℓ≥0.\left\|g-g_{\ell}\right\|_{L^{1}(0,\infty)}\leq C_{g}\Delta t_{\ell}^{\,{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{G}}},\hskip 18.49988pt\ell\geq 0. (22)
Proof.

We prove Proposition 2 in Appendix B. ∎

Under Assumptions 3, 4, and 5, and Conjecture 1, Proposition 2 yields Assumption 6 with p=pGp=p_{G}. The required global domination is not proved for the direct Adams implementation.

The fractional Adams scheme.

We solve the Volterra formulation (9) of the fractional Riccati equation (7) using the fractional Adams predictor-corrector method introduced in [16], as applied to the rough Heston model in [20]. Let tj=j​Δ​tt_{j}=j\Delta t, j=0,…,Mj=0,\ldots,M, with M​Δ​t=TM\Delta t=T, and let hΔ​t​(ξ,tj)h_{\Delta t}(\xi,t_{j}) denote the corresponding approximation of h⁡(ξ,tj)h(\xi,t_{j}).

At time step jj, the direct Adams implementation evaluates history sums over the preceding time points. Summing this work over j=1,…,Mj=1,\ldots,M gives 𝒪⁡(M2)\mathcal{O}(M^{2}) operations for one Fourier quadrature point [31, 14]. Once the nodal Riccati values are available, evaluating the composite trapezoidal rule in the fully discrete characteristic function exponent requires 𝒪⁡(M)\mathcal{O}(M) additional operations. Consequently, the total cost per characteristic-function evaluation is 𝒪⁡(M2+M)=𝒪⁡(M2)\mathcal{O}(M^{2}+M)=\mathcal{O}(M^{2}). Thus, the implementation used in this work has exponent β=2\beta=2 in the cost model. The generic analysis below retains β\beta so that it also applies to solvers with different cost estimates.

For the fractional Adams implementation, Assumption 3 is used with a generic nodal convergence exponent q>0q>0. We do not provide a theoretical value of qq for the fractional Adams scheme in the present setting. Proposition 2 then yields the Fourier-integrand rate p=pG=min⁡{q,rT}p=p_{G}=\min\{q,r_{T}\}.

In what follows, the analysis uses the generic exponent pp of Assumption 6 and the exponent β>0\beta>0 in the solver cost model, defined by Wℓ=𝒪⁡(Δ​tℓ−β)W_{\ell}=\mathcal{O}(\Delta t_{\ell}^{-\beta}). The results therefore apply to any solver for which such a pair (p,β)(p,\beta) is available. For the direct fractional Adams implementation used in this work, only the cost exponent is specialized theoretically, namely β=2\beta=2.

Remark 1 (Observed rate).

The numerical experiments in Section 4.1 indicate that the measured integrated Riccati and Fourier-integrand errors converge with slopes close to 1+α1+\alpha for the tested configurations. This observed rate is consistent with a convergence rate available for the fractional Adams method in [31] under assumptions that we do not verify in this work. Accordingly, we use 1+α1+\alpha as an empirical rate in the numerical estimators, while keeping qq, rTr_{T}, and pp generic in the theoretical analysis.

3.2 Single-Level Fourier Gauss-Laguerre Quadrature Method

In this section, we design a single-level Fourier pricing method based on a scaled Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule for the option value (1) with error control. The approximation combines a time discretization of (9), which controls the error of each evaluation of the characteristic function, with a Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule, which determines the number of such evaluations. The two choices are coupled because each quadrature point requires one solve of (9), so the discretization level fixes the cost per characteristic function evaluation while the Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule fixes the number of quadrature points. We prescribe a total tolerance ε>0\varepsilon>0, decompose the error into a discretization and a quadrature contribution, and allocate the tolerance between them. We then select the scaling factor of the scaled Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule in (37), the discretization level in (50), and the number of quadrature points in (51), and we derive the resulting computational complexity in Proposition 6.

In practice, unavailable quantities in the error bounds are replaced by Richardson-type indicators and fitted quadrature models; attainment of the target tolerance is therefore assessed numerically rather than certified a posteriori.

Gauss-Laguerre quadrature is a natural choice for the semi-infinite integral in (3). This choice is further supported by the behaviour of the integrand at large values of uu. In fact, it is conjectured and numerically supported in [12] that characteristic function of the rough Heston model decays exponentially along the integration contour with a rate determined by the model parameters ΘX\Theta_{X} and the maturity TT.

3.2.1 The scaled Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule.

The standard Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule typically employed in the Fourier pricing literature [33, 35, 6, 12] is associated with the weight function e−ue^{-u}. However, the effective decay rate of the integrand gg can be heavily affected by the model parameters, the maturity, the damping parameter, and the payoff parameters, as shown in [11] for several Lévy models. We refer also to Section 4.2 for numerical evidence in the rough Heston setting. We therefore introduce a scaling factor σ~>0\tilde{\sigma}>0, replacing the weight e−ue^{-u} by e−σ~​ue^{-\tilde{\sigma}u}. Since the quadrature is then applied to the transformed integrand eσ~​u​g​(u)e^{\tilde{\sigma}u}g(u), we choose the factor σ~\tilde{\sigma} heuristically to reflect the estimated asymptotic decay of the characteristic function.

We fix σ~>0\tilde{\sigma}>0 throughout and denote by {un,wn}n=1N\{u_{n},w_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N} the nodes and weights of the NN-point Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule associated with the weight e−σ~​ue^{-\tilde{\sigma}u} on (0,∞)(0,\infty); the dependence on σ~\tilde{\sigma} is left implicit. We refer to this as the scaled Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule [36]. It is the particular case of the generalized Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule, whose weight function is uλ​e−σ~​uu^{\lambda}e^{-\tilde{\sigma}u} with λ=0\lambda=0. Selecting σ~\tilde{\sigma} to match the decay of the integrand follows the domain transformation principle of [11], where the transformation is chosen to reproduce the functional form of the asymptotically dominant part of the Fourier integrand.

Writing

∫0∞gℓ​(u)​𝑑u=∫0∞e−σ~​u​g~ℓ​(u)​𝑑u,g~ℓ​(u):=eσ~​u​gℓ​(u),\int_{0}^{\infty}g_{\ell}(u)\,du=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\tilde{\sigma}u}\,\tilde{g}_{\ell}(u)\,du,\hskip 18.49988pt\tilde{g}_{\ell}(u):=e^{\tilde{\sigma}u}g_{\ell}(u), (23)

and absorbing the factor 22 of (3) into the quadrature approximation, we define

𝒬Nσ~​[gℓ]:=2​∑n=1Nwn​g~ℓ​(un),\mathcal{Q}_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}[g_{\ell}]:=2\sum_{n=1}^{N}w_{n}\,\tilde{g}_{\ell}(u_{n}), (24)

so that 𝒬Nσ~​[gℓ]\mathcal{Q}_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}[g_{\ell}] approximates 2​∫0∞gℓ​(u)​𝑑u2\int_{0}^{\infty}g_{\ell}(u)\,du. The standard Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule corresponds to σ~=1\tilde{\sigma}=1. Increasing σ~\tilde{\sigma} concentrates the nodes near the origin; decreasing σ~\tilde{\sigma} spreads them towards larger values of uu. We write

RNσ~​(gℓ):=2​∫0∞gℓ​(u)​𝑑u−𝒬Nσ~​[gℓ]R_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(g_{\ell}):=2\int_{0}^{\infty}g_{\ell}(u)\,du-\mathcal{Q}_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}[g_{\ell}] (25)

for the quadrature remainder of the scaled Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule (24) at level ℓ\ell, and |RNσ~​(gℓ)|\left|R_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(g_{\ell})\right| for the corresponding quadrature error.

3.2.2 Error analysis of the single-level method.

We now approximate the option value VV by combining the time discretization of Section 3.1 with the scaled Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule (24), and split the resulting error into the two contributions that determine the choice of LL and NN. We denote by

Vℓ:=2​∫0∞gℓ​(u)​𝑑uV_{\ell}:=2\int_{0}^{\infty}g_{\ell}(u)\,du (26)

the value obtained by replacing Φ\Phi with Φℓ\Phi_{\ell} in (3), and by VN,ℓ:=𝒬Nσ~​[gℓ]V_{N,\ell}:=\mathcal{Q}_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}[g_{\ell}] its approximation by the scaled Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule (24) with NN quadrature points. The single-level approximation at level LL is thus VN,LV_{N,L}. Adding and subtracting VLV_{L} gives

|V−VN,L|≤|V−VL|⏟=:edisc​(L)+|VL−VN,L|⏟=:equad​(N,L),\left|V-V_{N,L}\right|\;\leq\;\underbrace{\left|V-V_{L}\right|}_{=:\;e_{\mathrm{disc}}(L)}\;+\;\underbrace{\left|V_{L}-V_{N,L}\right|}_{=:\;e_{\mathrm{quad}}(N,L)}, (27)

where we recall that V=V⁡(ΘX,ΘP)V=V(\Theta_{X},\Theta_{P}). The first term is the error of the time discretization and depends on LL only. By (3), (26) and Assumption 6,

edisc​(L)=2​|∫0∞(g⁡(u)−gL​(u))​𝑑u|≤2​‖g−gL‖L1​(0,∞)≤2​Cg​Δ​tLp.e_{\mathrm{disc}}(L)=2\left|\int_{0}^{\infty}\bigl(g(u)-g_{L}(u)\bigr)\,du\right|\leq 2\left\|g-g_{L}\right\|_{L^{1}(0,\infty)}\leq 2C_{g}\Delta t_{L}^{\,p}.

The second term is the error from the Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule at the fixed level LL, that is, equad​(N,L)=|RNσ~​(gL)|e_{\mathrm{quad}}(N,L)=|R_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(g_{L})| defined in (25). Given a tolerance ε>0\varepsilon>0, we split the error as follows ε=εdisc+εquad\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{disc}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}} and require

edisc​(L)≤εdisc,equad​(N,L)≤εquad.e_{\mathrm{disc}}(L)\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{disc}},\hskip 18.49988pte_{\mathrm{quad}}(N,L)\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}}. (28)

Unless stated otherwise we take εdisc=εquad=ε/2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{disc}}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}}=\varepsilon/2. Each of the NN terms in (24) requires one solve of (9) at cost WL=𝒪⁡(Δ​tL−β)W_{L}=\mathcal{O}(\Delta t_{L}^{-\beta}). Thus, the computational work required by the single-level method is

WSL​(N,L):=N​WL.W_{\mathrm{SL}}(N,L):=NW_{L}. (29)

We fix σ~\tilde{\sigma} first, and then select LL and NN from the two constraints in (28). Before selecting them, we recall the estimates available for the Gauss-Laguerre quadrature remainder (25).

Analysis of the Gauss-Laguerre quadrature error.

We consider both algebraic and root-exponential estimates for the Gauss-Laguerre quadrature error. As observed numerically in Section 4.2.2, the root-exponential estimate provides a closer description of the quadrature errors, whereas the algebraic estimate is more conservative. The algebraic estimate, however, permits the explicit optimization and complexity analysis developed in Propositions 4, 8, 6, and 9, including the closed-form expression for the minimum multilevel work in (66).

The algebraic estimate is applied to the real transformed integrand g~ℓ\tilde{g}_{\ell} defined in (23). For the root-exponential estimate, analyticity is instead imposed on the underlying complex transformed integrand

f~ℓ​(z):=eσ~​z​e−r​T2​π​Φℓ​(z+i​R)​P^​(z+i​R),g~ℓ​(u)=ℜ⁡f~ℓ​(u),u≥0.\tilde{f}_{\ell}(z):=e^{\tilde{\sigma}z}\frac{e^{-rT}}{2\pi}\Phi_{\ell}(z+\mathrm{i}R)\widehat{P}(z+\mathrm{i}R),\hskip 18.49988pt\tilde{g}_{\ell}(u)=\Re\tilde{f}_{\ell}(u),\hskip 9.24994ptu\geq 0. (30)

Both estimates are stated at a fixed level ℓ\ell, hence for a fixed Δ​tℓ\Delta t_{\ell}.

Assumption 7 (Regularity of the transformed integrand).

Let σ~>0\tilde{\sigma}>0 and ℓ∈ℕ0\ell\in\mathbb{N}_{0}. There exists an integer sℓ≥1s_{\ell}\geq 1 such that

g~ℓ(sℓ−1)∈A​Cloc​(0,∞),∫0∞usℓ/2​|g~ℓ(sℓ)​(u)|​e−σ~​u​𝑑u<∞.\tilde{g}_{\ell}^{(s_{\ell}-1)}\in AC_{\mathrm{loc}}(0,\infty),\hskip 18.49988pt\int_{0}^{\infty}u^{s_{\ell}/2}\left|\tilde{g}_{\ell}^{(s_{\ell})}(u)\right|e^{-\tilde{\sigma}u}\,du<\infty.
Theorem 1 ([32]).

Let Assumption 7 hold at level ℓ\ell. Then there exists a constant Csℓ,σ~>0C_{s_{\ell},\tilde{\sigma}}>0, independent of NN, such that

|RNσ~(gℓ)|≤AℓN−sℓ/2,N≥1,\left|R_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(g_{\ell})\right|\leq A_{\ell}\,N^{-s_{\ell}/2},\hskip 18.49988ptN\geq 1, (31)

where

Aℓ:=Csℓ,σ~​∫0∞usℓ/2​|g~ℓ(sℓ)​(u)|​e−σ~​u​𝑑u.A_{\ell}:=C_{s_{\ell},\tilde{\sigma}}\int_{0}^{\infty}u^{s_{\ell}/2}\left|\tilde{g}_{\ell}^{(s_{\ell})}(u)\right|e^{-\tilde{\sigma}u}\,du.

The estimate in [32] is stated for the standard Laguerre weight e−ue^{-u}. The form (31) follows by rescaling the nodes and weights as in (24); the fixed factors introduced by this rescaling are absorbed into Csℓ,σ~C_{s_{\ell},\tilde{\sigma}}. We let sℓs_{\ell} be the smoothness index and AℓA_{\ell} the constant in the error estimate. The second estimate replaces the finite regularity of Assumption 7 by analyticity and growth conditions on the complex transformed integrand f~ℓ\tilde{f}_{\ell}, and yields a rate in NN faster than any algebraic one.

Assumption 8 (Analyticity of the complex transformed integrand).

Let R∈δVR\in\delta_{V}, σ~>0\tilde{\sigma}>0, and ℓ∈ℕ0\ell\in\mathbb{N}_{0}. Assume that f~ℓ\tilde{f}_{\ell} defined in (30) is analytic in the interior of a parabola containing the positive real axis and continuous on its boundary. Assume further that there exist constants Can,ℓ<∞C_{\mathrm{an},\ell}<\infty and mℓ∈ℝm_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R} such that

|f~ℓ​(z)|≤Can,ℓ​|z|mℓ\left|\tilde{f}_{\ell}(z)\right|\leq C_{\mathrm{an},\ell}\,|z|^{m_{\ell}}

as |z|→∞|z|\to\infty in the interior of that parabola.

Define the corresponding complex quadrature remainder by

ℛNσ~​(f~ℓ):=2​∫0∞e−σ~​u​f~ℓ​(u)​𝑑u−2​∑n=1Nwn​f~ℓ​(un).\mathcal{R}_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(\tilde{f}_{\ell}):=2\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\tilde{\sigma}u}\tilde{f}_{\ell}(u)\,du-2\sum_{n=1}^{N}w_{n}\tilde{f}_{\ell}(u_{n}). (32)

Since g~ℓ​(u)=ℜ⁡f~ℓ​(u)\tilde{g}_{\ell}(u)=\Re\tilde{f}_{\ell}(u) and the quadrature weights are real,

RNσ~​(gℓ)=ℜ⁡[ℛNσ~​(f~ℓ)].R_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(g_{\ell})=\Re\!\left[\mathcal{R}_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(\tilde{f}_{\ell})\right]. (33)
Theorem 2 ([36]).

Let Assumption 8 hold at level ℓ\ell. Then there exist constants Aℓre<∞A_{\ell}^{\mathrm{re}}<\infty and Bℓ>0B_{\ell}>0 such that

|ℛNσ~​(f~ℓ)|≤Aℓre​exp⁡(−Bℓ​N),N≥1.\left|\mathcal{R}_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(\tilde{f}_{\ell})\right|\leq A_{\ell}^{\mathrm{re}}\exp\!\left(-B_{\ell}\sqrt{N}\right),\hskip 18.49988ptN\geq 1. (34)

Consequently,

|RNσ~​(gℓ)|≤Aℓre​exp⁡(−Bℓ​N),N≥1.\left|R_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(g_{\ell})\right|\leq A_{\ell}^{\mathrm{re}}\exp\!\left(-B_{\ell}\sqrt{N}\right),\hskip 18.49988ptN\geq 1. (35)

The estimate in Theorem 6.3 of [36] is stated for the standard Laguerre weight e−ue^{-u} and for all sufficiently large NN. Rescaling the nodes and weights as in (24) gives (34), with the fixed factors absorbed into AℓreA_{\ell}^{\mathrm{re}} and BℓB_{\ell}. For each fixed level ℓ\ell, AℓreA_{\ell}^{\mathrm{re}} can be increased to cover the finitely many remaining positive integers. The real estimate (35) then follows from (33). Such an analyticity condition is consistent with those used for contour deformations in Fourier pricing [12], but is not available in closed form for the rough Heston model and is therefore assumed. The parabola and the growth condition depend on σ~\tilde{\sigma} and the damping parameter RR.

3.2.3 Numerical parameter selection for the single-level method

Scaling factor.

The nodes of the scaled Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule (24) are those of the standard Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule divided by σ~\tilde{\sigma}, so σ~\tilde{\sigma} determines the range of values of uu at which the integrand is evaluated. We therefore choose σ~\tilde{\sigma} heuristically to reflect the estimated decay rate of gg, which is primarily determined by the characteristic function. In addition, by the explicit formula for P^\widehat{P} in Section 2.2, we know that the payoff transform contributes an algebraic factor and does not affect the exponential decay rate [30]. As |ξ|→∞|\xi|\to\infty along the contour, it is conjectured in [12] that the solution of (9) behaves as h⁡(ξ,τ)=h∞​ξ+𝒪⁡(1)h(\xi,\tau)=h_{\infty}\xi+\mathcal{O}(1) with h∞=−(iρ+1−ρ2)/(γν)h_{\infty}=-(\mathrm{i}\rho+\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}})/(\gamma\nu), and that the characteristic function exponent (10) satisfies (G⁡(ξ)−i​ξ​(X0+r​T))/ξ→−c∞​(T)\bigl(G(\xi)-\mathrm{i}\xi(X_{0}+rT)\bigr)/\xi\to-c_{\infty}(T) with

Re⁡c∞​(T)=1−ρ2γ​ν​(γ​θ​T+V0​T1−αΓ⁡(2−α)),\operatorname{Re}c_{\infty}(T)=\frac{\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}}}{\gamma\nu}\left(\gamma\theta T+\frac{V_{0}\,T^{1-\alpha}}{\Gamma(2-\alpha)}\right), (36)

under which |Φ⁡(u+i​R)||\Phi(u+\mathrm{i}R)| decays like e−Re⁡c∞​(T)​ue^{-\operatorname{Re}c_{\infty}(T)u}. This conjectured asymptotic behaviour is supported by the numerical experiments in [12] and motivates the choice

σ~:=Re⁡c∞​(T).\tilde{\sigma}:=\operatorname{Re}c_{\infty}(T). (37)

For |ρ|<1|\rho|<1, this choice aligns the exponential weight with the estimated large-uu decay of the Fourier integrand. At |ρ|=1|\rho|=1, the scale degenerates to zero; these endpoint cases are not considered here and would require a separate positive scale. Relative to this estimate, the standard Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule can leave g~\tilde{g} exponentially growing at short maturities and can place its nodes over an unnecessarily wide range of uu at long maturities. The resulting loss of accuracy at short maturities and at strikes far from the spot price is documented in [12]. Section 4.2 provides corresponding numerical evidence for the parameter sets considered here.

Discretization level.

By Assumption 6, the discretization error satisfies edisc​(L)≤2​Cg​Δ​tLpe_{\mathrm{disc}}(L)\leq 2C_{g}\Delta t_{L}^{\,p}, so the first constraint in (28) is satisfied whenever Δ​tL≤(εdisc/2​Cg)1/p\Delta t_{L}\leq(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{disc}}/2C_{g})^{1/p}. Since Δ​tℓ=2−ℓ​Δ​t0\Delta t_{\ell}=2^{-\ell}\Delta t_{0}, this is equivalent to

ℓ≥1p​log2⁡(2​Cg​Δ​t0pεdisc),\ell\geq\frac{1}{p}\log_{2}\!\left(\frac{2C_{g}\Delta t_{0}^{\,p}}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{disc}}}\right),

and the smallest required theoretical level is

⌈1p​log2⁡(2​Cg​Δ​t0pεdisc)⌉,{\left\lceil\frac{1}{p}\log_{2}\!\left(\frac{2C_{g}\Delta t_{0}^{\,p}}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{disc}}}\right)\right\rceil}, (38)

where ⌈x⌉\lceil x\rceil denotes the smallest integer greater than or equal to x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. The constant CgC_{g} of Assumption 6 is not available, so (38) is used in the complexity analysis rather than in the computations. To derive a practical rule for selecting the level LL, we instead use a Richardson estimator based on the difference between two consecutive levels. By the definitions of VV and VℓV_{\ell} in (3) and (26), respectively,

|Vℓ−V|=2​|∫0∞(g−gℓ)​(u)​𝑑u|≤2​‖g−gℓ‖L1​(0,∞),|V_{\ell}-V|=2\left|\int_{0}^{\infty}(g-g_{\ell})(u)\,du\right|\leq 2\|g-g_{\ell}\|_{L^{1}(0,\infty)},

However, this bound only shows that the price error is at most of order Δ​tℓp\Delta t_{\ell}^{\,p}; it does not guarantee that the price error is asymptotically proportional to Δ​tℓp\Delta t_{\ell}^{\,p}. Positive and negative parts of g−gℓg-g_{\ell} may cancel after integration, producing a smaller leading price error. The following assumption rules out this cancellation and provides the leading-order expansion required by the Richardson estimator.

Assumption 9 (Sharp price-discretization expansion).

There exists a constant cV≠0c_{V}\neq 0 such that

Vℓ−V=cV​Δ​tℓp+o⁡(Δ​tℓp),ℓ→∞,V_{\ell}-V=c_{V}\Delta t_{\ell}^{\,p}+o\!\left(\Delta t_{\ell}^{\,p}\right),\hskip 18.49988pt\ell\to\infty, (39)

where p>0p>0 is the exponent in Assumption 6. Thus, the price has the same leading convergence order as the L1L^{1} integrand error, with no cancellation of its leading contribution after integration.

Assumption 9 is stronger than Assumption 6 and is used only to justify the Richardson estimator; it is not used in Propositions 6–9.

We provide numerical evidence for Assumption 9 in Section 4.1. Under this assumption, Proposition 3 relates the discretization error to the difference between two consecutive levels and thereby yields a computable rule for selecting LL.

Proposition 3 (Asymptotic Richardson error estimate).

Let Δ​tℓ=2−ℓ​Δ​t0\Delta t_{\ell}=2^{-\ell}\Delta t_{0} and suppose that Assumption 9 holds. Define the price error and its Richardson estimator by

EℓV:=edisc​(ℓ)=|V−Vℓ|,E^ℓV:=|Vℓ−Vℓ−1|2p−1.E_{\ell}^{\,V}:=e_{\mathrm{disc}}(\ell)=|V-V_{\ell}|,\hskip 18.49988pt\widehat{E}_{\ell}^{\,V}:=\frac{|V_{\ell}-V_{\ell-1}|}{2^{\,p}-1}. (40)

Then

EℓV=E^ℓV​(1+o⁡(1)),ℓ→∞.E_{\ell}^{\,V}=\widehat{E}_{\ell}^{\,V}\left(1+o(1)\right),\hskip 18.49988pt\ell\to\infty. (41)
Proof.

We prove Proposition 3 in Appendix C. ∎

For the computable approximations, define the signed quadrature error

qN,ℓ:=VN,ℓ−Vℓ.q_{N,\ell}:=V_{N,\ell}-V_{\ell}. (42)

Suppose that VN,ℓV_{N,\ell} and VN,ℓ−1V_{N,\ell-1} are evaluated with the same scaled Gauss–Laguerre rule, that is, with the same NN, scaling parameter σ~\tilde{\sigma}, nodes, and weights. By linearity of the quadrature rule, the quadrature perturbation of the level difference is

eN,ℓΔ\displaystyle e_{N,\ell}^{\Delta} :=|(VN,ℓ−VN,ℓ−1)−(Vℓ−Vℓ−1)|\displaystyle:=\left|(V_{N,\ell}-V_{N,\ell-1})-(V_{\ell}-V_{\ell-1})\right| (43)
=|qN,ℓ−qN,ℓ−1|=|RNσ~​(gℓ−gℓ−1)|.\displaystyle=\left|q_{N,\ell}-q_{N,\ell-1}\right|=\left|R_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(g_{\ell}-g_{\ell-1})\right|.

Consequently, the reverse triangle inequality gives

||VN,ℓ−VN,ℓ−1|−|Vℓ−Vℓ−1||≤eN,ℓΔ=|RNσ~​(gℓ−gℓ−1)|.\bigl||V_{N,\ell}-V_{N,\ell-1}|-|V_{\ell}-V_{\ell-1}|\bigr|\leq e_{N,\ell}^{\Delta}=\left|R_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(g_{\ell}-g_{\ell-1})\right|. (44)

Suppose that, for the chosen quadrature order NN, there exists a constant CQ,N<∞C_{Q,N}<\infty, independent of ℓ\ell, such that

|RNσ~​(gℓ−gℓ−1)|≤CQ,N​Δ​tℓp.\left|R_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(g_{\ell}-g_{\ell-1})\right|\leq C_{Q,N}\Delta t_{\ell}^{\,p}. (45)

Define the computable Richardson estimator by

E^N,ℓV:=|VN,ℓ−VN,ℓ−1|2p−1.\widehat{E}_{N,\ell}^{\,V}:=\frac{|V_{N,\ell}-V_{N,\ell-1}|}{2^{p}-1}. (46)

Proposition 3 and (44) then give

|edisc​(ℓ)−E^N,ℓV|≤CQ,N2p−1​Δ​tℓp+o⁡(Δ​tℓp).\left|e_{\mathrm{disc}}(\ell)-\widehat{E}_{N,\ell}^{\,V}\right|\leq\frac{C_{Q,N}}{2^{p}-1}\Delta t_{\ell}^{\,p}+o\!\left(\Delta t_{\ell}^{\,p}\right). (47)

Thus, the accuracy of the computable Richardson estimator then depends on CQ,NC_{Q,N} being small relative to the leading level-difference coefficient (2p−1)​|cV|(2^{p}-1)|c_{V}|. The theoretical complexity analysis continues to use the certified L1L^{1} bound and level (38); the rule below is its practical, asymptotic replacement.

Evaluating this Richardson error estimate at every level would require the corresponding level approximations. Instead, we compute the first level difference with N¯comp\bar{N}^{\mathrm{comp}} quadrature points and define

D1:=|VN¯comp,1−VN¯comp,0|.D_{1}:=\left|{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}V_{\bar{N}^{\mathrm{comp}},1}-V_{\bar{N}^{\mathrm{comp}},0}}\right|. (48)

For ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, we use the asymptotic Richardson-type discretization indicator

ηdisc​(ℓ):=D12p−1​2−p⁡(ℓ−1).\eta_{\mathrm{disc}}(\ell):=\frac{D_{1}}{2^{\,p}-1}2^{-p(\ell-1)}. (49)

This asymptotic indicator extrapolates the asymptotic rate from the first level difference and is not a certified error bound unless levels 00 and 11 are already in the asymptotic regime and the quadrature error of their level difference is sufficiently small. Accordingly, Δ​t0\Delta t_{0} must be chosen sufficiently small that D1D_{1} is numerically stable under further time refinement. We select the smallest level L≥1L\geq 1 satisfying ηdisc​(L)≤εdisc\eta_{\mathrm{disc}}(L)\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{disc}}, namely

L:=max⁡{1,⌈1+1p​log2⁡(D1(2p−1)​εdisc)⌉}.L:={\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\max\!\Biggl\{1,}{\left\lceil 1+\frac{1}{p}\log_{2}\!\left(\frac{D_{1}}{\left(2^{\,p}-1\right)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{disc}}}\right)\right\rceil}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\Biggr\}}. (50)

The behaviour of this level selection rule is assessed in Section 4.

Number of quadrature points.

The level LL is fixed by (50). The second constraint in (28) is then a separate condition on NN. We select NN differently based on the used quadrature error estimate.

Remark 2 (Relation between the two quadrature estimates).

We note that the two estimates are not interchangeable. If the quadrature error satisfies (35), then, for every fixed s>0s>0, it also satisfies an estimate of the form (31) with a suitable constant and for NN large enough. However, the converse does not hold. The algebraic estimate is in this sense the conservative one, and the number of quadrature points it selects through (51) exceeds the number selected by Proposition 5 for εquad\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}} small enough. Where (35) holds, the latter therefore gives the sharper estimate of the work required to reach a prescribed tolerance.

Proposition 4 (Number of quadrature points under the algebraic error estimate).

Let Assumption 7 hold at level LL and let εquad>0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}}>0. Then every N≥NalgN\geq N_{\mathrm{alg}} satisfies the quadrature constraint in (28), where

Nalg:=⌈(ALεquad)2/sL⌉.N_{\mathrm{alg}}:={\left\lceil\left(\frac{A_{L}}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}}}\right)^{2/s_{L}}\right\rceil}. (51)

Moreover, NalgN_{\mathrm{alg}} is the smallest integer number of quadrature points certified by the algebraic estimate (31) to satisfy the constraint.

Proof.

By (31), the quadrature constraint holds whenever N≥(AL/εquad)2/sLN\geq(A_{L}/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}})^{2/s_{L}}. Therefore, (51) is the smallest integer certified by (31), and every larger integer also satisfies the constraint. ∎

Under Assumption 8, the corresponding certified number of quadrature points is obtained by inverting the root-exponential error estimate.

Proposition 5 (Number of quadrature points under the root-exponential error estimate).

Let Assumption 8 hold for fixed LL and let 0<εquad<ALre0<\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}}<A_{L}^{\mathrm{re}}. Then every N≥NreN\geq N_{\mathrm{re}} satisfies the quadrature constraint in (28), where

Nre:=⌈1BL2​log2⁡(ALreεquad)⌉.N_{\mathrm{re}}:=\left\lceil\frac{1}{B_{L}^{2}}\log^{2}\!\left(\frac{A_{L}^{\mathrm{re}}}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}}}\right)\right\rceil. (52)

Moreover, NreN_{\mathrm{re}} is the smallest integer number of quadrature points certified by the root-exponential estimate (35) to satisfy the constraint.

Proof.

By (35), the quadrature constraint holds whenever ALre​exp⁡(−BL​N)≤εquadA_{L}^{\mathrm{re}}\exp(-B_{L}\sqrt{N})\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}}. Since 0<εquad<ALre0<\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}}<A_{L}^{\mathrm{re}}, this sufficient condition is equivalent to N≥BL−2​log2⁡(ALre/εquad)N\geq B_{L}^{-2}\log^{2}(A_{L}^{\mathrm{re}}/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}}). Therefore, (52) is the smallest integer certified by (35), and every larger integer also satisfies the constraint. ∎

Remark 3 (Practical estimation of the quadrature parameters).

The theoretical selection rules (51) and (52) use the quadrature parameters at the selected finest level LL. Estimating these parameters directly would require repeated quadrature computations at the most expensive discretization level. In practice, we instead estimate the algebraic parameters A0A_{0} and s0s_{0} and the root-exponential parameters A0reA_{0}^{\mathrm{re}} and B0B_{0} at level zero, and use them as surrogates for ALA_{L}, sLs_{L}, ALreA_{L}^{\mathrm{re}}, and BLB_{L}, respectively. Section 4.2.2, in particular Figure 10, provides numerical evidence that these parameters vary only weakly across the discretization levels considered. This replacement is an empirical implementation choice and is not part of the certified bounds in Propositions 4 and 5, which retain the actual level-LL parameters.

As εquad→0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}}\to 0, the number of quadrature points selected by (51) grows algebraically in 1/εquad1/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}}, whereas (52) grows as log2⁡(1/εquad)\log^{2}(1/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}}).

We study how the computational work required by the proposed single-level method scales as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0.

Proposition 6 (Complexity of the single-level method under the algebraic quadrature error estimate).

Let Assumption 6 hold. Suppose that there exist an integer sSL≥1s_{\mathrm{SL}}\geq 1, a constant A<∞A<\infty and ε0>0\varepsilon_{0}>0 such that, for every ε∈(0,ε0]\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_{0}], Assumption 7 holds at level L⁡(ε)L(\varepsilon) with

sL⁡(ε)≥sSL,AL⁡(ε)≤A.{s_{L(\varepsilon)}\geq s_{\mathrm{SL}}},\hskip 18.49988ptA_{L(\varepsilon)}\leq A.

Assume that Assumption 8 holds at level LL and that 0<εquad<ALre0<\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}}<A_{L}^{\mathrm{re}}. Let N=NreN=N_{\mathrm{re}} be given by Proposition 5. AL⁡(ε)re≤Are,BL⁡(ε)≥B.A_{L(\varepsilon)}^{\mathrm{re}}\leq A^{\mathrm{re}},\hskip 18.49988ptB_{L(\varepsilon)}\geq B.

3.3 Multilevel Fourier Gauss-Laguerre Quadrature Method

In this section, we design a multilevel Fourier pricing method based on the scaled Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule for the option value (1). The single-level method of Section 3.2 evaluates the integrand at every quadrature point at the level LL selected by (50), so all NN solves of (9) are performed at the finest and most expensive level. The multilevel method instead splits the integrand into a level zero term and a hierarchy of level differences, and applies the scaled Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule to each. The number of quadrature points is then chosen separately at each level such that the total work is minimized by distributing the quadrature points across the hierarchy, placing few of them at the levels where one evaluation is expensive, and more quadrature points where the fractional Riccati equation is solved at a coarser mesh. The level LL remains given by (50), and the quadrature tolerance εquad\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}} of (28) is distributed among the levels. We state the assumptions on the regularity and the level decay of the level differences, derive the allocation of the quadrature points, and obtain the resulting computational complexity in Proposition 9.

We first write the integrand at level LL as a telescoping sum. For ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1 we define the level differences

Δ​gℓ:=gℓ−gℓ−1,Δ​g~ℓ:=g~ℓ−g~ℓ−1,\Delta g_{\ell}:=g_{\ell}-g_{\ell-1},\hskip 18.49988pt\Delta\tilde{g}_{\ell}:=\tilde{g}_{\ell}-\tilde{g}_{\ell-1}, (55)

with g~ℓ\tilde{g}_{\ell} given by (23), and we set the level-zero integrands g0g_{0} and g~0\tilde{g}_{0} apart from the level differences. Derivatives of the level differences are denoted for m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} by (Δ​g~ℓ)(m)=g~ℓ(m)−g~ℓ−1(m)\left(\Delta\tilde{g}_{\ell}\right)^{(m)}=\tilde{g}_{\ell}^{(m)}-\tilde{g}_{\ell-1}^{(m)}. By definition of (55),

gL=g0+∑ℓ=1LΔ​gℓ.{g_{L}=g_{0}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\Delta g_{\ell}.} (56)

Let 𝐍:=(N0,…,NL)\mathbf{N}:=(N_{0},\ldots,N_{L}), with Nℓ≥1N_{\ell}\geq 1 for every ℓ\ell. Applying the scaled Gauss-Laguerre quadrature rule (24) with N0N_{0} quadrature points to g0g_{0} and with NℓN_{\ell} quadrature points to Δ​gℓ\Delta g_{\ell} for ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, we define the multilevel approximation

V𝐍,L:=𝒬N0σ~​[g0]+∑ℓ=1L𝒬Nℓσ~​[Δ​gℓ].{V_{\mathbf{N},L}:=\mathcal{Q}_{N_{0}}^{\tilde{\sigma}}[g_{0}]+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathcal{Q}_{N_{\ell}}^{\tilde{\sigma}}[\Delta g_{\ell}].} (57)

For ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, evaluating Δ​gℓ\Delta g_{\ell} at one quadrature point requires one solve of (9) at level ℓ\ell and one at level ℓ−1\ell-1, at a cost of Wℓ+Wℓ−1W_{\ell}+W_{\ell-1}. The level-zero term costs W0W_{0} per quadrature point. The computational work required by the multilevel method is

WML​(𝐍,L)=W0​N0+∑ℓ=1L(Wℓ+Wℓ−1)​Nℓ.{W_{\mathrm{ML}}(\mathbf{N},L)=W_{0}N_{0}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\left(W_{\ell}+W_{\ell-1}\right)N_{\ell}.} (58)

3.3.1 Error analysis and practical parameter selection for the multilevel method

We now split the error of (57) into the two contributions of (27). Adding and subtracting VLV_{L} gives

|V−V𝐍,L|≤|V−VL|⏟=edisc​(L)+|VL−V𝐍,L|⏟=:equad​(𝐍,L).\left|V-V_{\mathbf{N},L}\right|\;\leq\;\underbrace{\left|V-V_{L}\right|}_{=\;e_{\mathrm{disc}}(L)}\;+\;\underbrace{\left|V_{L}-V_{\mathbf{N},L}\right|}_{=:\;e_{\mathrm{quad}}(\mathbf{N},L)}. (59)

The discretization error is unchanged, and LL is therefore selected by (50). The Richardson estimate of Proposition 3, together with the condition on the quadrature errors stated after that proposition, applies without modification. By (26), (56), (57) and (25),

VL−V𝐍,L=RN0σ~​(g0)+∑ℓ=1LRNℓσ~​(Δ​gℓ).{V_{L}-V_{\mathbf{N},L}=R_{N_{0}}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(g_{0})+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}R_{N_{\ell}}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(\Delta g_{\ell}).}

hence

equad​(𝐍,L)≤|RN0σ~​(g0)|+∑ℓ=1L|RNℓσ~​(Δ​gℓ)|.{e_{\mathrm{quad}}(\mathbf{N},L)\leq|R_{N_{0}}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(g_{0})|+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\left|R_{N_{\ell}}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(\Delta g_{\ell})\right|.} (60)

We impose on the level differences the regularity required by Theorem 1.

Assumption 10 (Regularity of the level differences).

Let σ~>0\tilde{\sigma}>0 and ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N}. There exists an integer sℓ≥1s_{\ell}\geq 1 such that

(Δ​g~ℓ)(sℓ−1)∈A​Cloc​(0,∞),∫0∞usℓ/2​|(Δ​g~ℓ)(sℓ)​(u)|​e−σ~​u​𝑑u<∞.\left(\Delta\tilde{g}_{\ell}\right)^{(s_{\ell}-1)}\in AC_{\mathrm{loc}}(0,\infty),\hskip 18.49988pt\int_{0}^{\infty}u^{s_{\ell}/2}\left|\left(\Delta\tilde{g}_{\ell}\right)^{(s_{\ell})}(u)\right|e^{-\tilde{\sigma}u}\,du<\infty.

At level zero, Assumption 7 with smoothness index s0s_{0} and Theorem 1 give

|RNσ~(g0)|≤A0N−s0/2.\left|R_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(g_{0})\right|\leq A_{0}N^{-s_{0}/2}.

For ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, Assumption 10 is Assumption 7 applied to the integrand Δ​gℓ\Delta g_{\ell}. Hence, Theorem 1 gives

There exists a constant CA<∞C_{A}<\infty, independent of ℓ\ell, such that the constants AℓA_{\ell} of (61) satisfy

Assumption 11 is separate from Assumption 6. The latter controls ‖g−gℓ‖L1​(0,∞)\|g-g_{\ell}\|_{L^{1}(0,\infty)}, whereas AℓA_{\ell} is defined in (61) by a weighted seminorm of the derivative of order sℓs_{\ell} of Δ​g~ℓ\Delta\tilde{g}_{\ell}. Section 4.2.2, in particular Figure 12, provides numerical evidence that the fitted constants AℓA_{\ell} decay with an exponent close to pp, supporting Assumption 11 for the levels considered.

3.3.2 Computational complexity.

The allocation (65) is valid for any prescribed tolerance. For the complexity estimate, we additionally assume s>2​p/βs>2p/\beta. Under this condition, the finest correction level determines the asymptotic order of the correction contribution in (66). The separate level-zero contribution has order 𝒪(ε−2/s0)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2/s_{0}}). For the direct fractional Adams scheme, β=2\beta=2, so the condition becomes s>ps>p. The numerical evidence in Section 4.2.2 indicates that the fitted effective regularity indices are above the corresponding thresholds for the parameter sets and finite-range convergence rates considered.

Wℓ≤CW​Δ​tℓ−β,ℓ≥0,W_{\ell}\leq C_{W}\Delta t_{\ell}^{-\beta},\hskip 18.49988pt\ell\geq 0, (67)

for some CW<∞C_{W}<\infty and β>0\beta>0. Suppose in addition that there exists an integer ss, independent of LL, satisfying (62) and s>2​p/βs>2p/\beta. |V−V𝐍,L|≤ε|V-V_{\mathbf{N},L}|\leq\varepsilon

If, in addition,

s0≥2​pβ,s_{0}\geq\frac{2p}{\beta},

then

WML(𝐍,L)=𝒪(ε−β/p),ε→0.{W_{\mathrm{ML}}(\mathbf{N},L)=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\varepsilon^{-\beta/p}\right),\hskip 18.49988pt\varepsilon\to 0.} (69)

We prove Proposition 9 in Appendix G.

Allocation of 𝐍\mathbf{N} under the root-exponential estimate.

The allocation of (65) is based on the algebraic error estimate (31), which we use mainly for the complexity analysis. In the numerical implementation we instead allocate the quadrature points based on the root-exponential quadrature error estimates observed for the level-zero term and the level differences. Let A0re>0A_{0}^{\mathrm{re}}>0 and B0>0B_{0}>0 denote the level-zero prefactor and rate. For the correction levels, let Aℓre>0A_{\ell}^{\mathrm{re}}>0 and Bℓ>0B_{\ell}>0 denote the corresponding prefactors and rates. Section 4.2.2, in particular Figure 11, provides numerical evidence that the fitted rates BℓB_{\ell} are approximately constant across the correction levels considered. We therefore use a common correction rate B>0B>0, that is, Bℓ=BB_{\ell}=B for ℓ=1,…,L\ell=1,\ldots,L, and write the empirical error estimates as

|RNσ~​(g0)|\displaystyle\left|R_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(g_{0})\right| ≤A0re​exp⁡(−B0​N),\displaystyle\leq A_{0}^{\mathrm{re}}\exp\!\left(-B_{0}\sqrt{N}\right), (70)
|RNσ~​(Δ​gℓ)|\displaystyle\left|R_{N}^{\tilde{\sigma}}(\Delta g_{\ell})\right| ≤Aℓreexp(−BN),ℓ=1,…,L.\displaystyle\leq A_{\ell}^{\mathrm{re}}\exp\!\left(-B\sqrt{N}\right),\hskip 18.49988pt\ell=1,\ldots,L.

We then determine the number of quadrature points at each level by solving

minN0,…,NL\displaystyle\min_{N_{0},\ldots,N_{L}} W0​N0+∑ℓ=1L(Wℓ+Wℓ−1)​Nℓ\displaystyle W_{0}N_{0}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\left(W_{\ell}+W_{\ell-1}\right)N_{\ell} (71)
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} A0re​exp⁡(−B0​N0)+∑ℓ=1LAℓre​exp⁡(−B​Nℓ)≤εquad,\displaystyle A_{0}^{\mathrm{re}}\exp\!\left(-B_{0}\sqrt{N_{0}}\right)+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}A_{\ell}^{\mathrm{re}}\exp\!\left(-B\sqrt{N_{\ell}}\right)\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}},
N0≥1,Nℓ≥1,ℓ=1,…,L.\displaystyle N_{0}\geq 1,\hskip 18.49988ptN_{\ell}\geq 1,\hskip 9.24994pt\ell=1,\ldots,L.

We solve the resulting problem (71) numerically, and take the ceilings of the resulting values, which preserves the constraint in (71) because each error term is decreasing in its corresponding number of quadrature points.

Remark 4 (Practical construction of the multilevel quadrature parameters).

The algebraic allocation (65) and the root-exponential optimization (71) involve the prefactors AℓA_{\ell} and AℓreA_{\ell}^{\mathrm{re}} at all correction levels. Fitting these prefactors separately would require pilot quadrature computations at every increasingly expensive level. In practice, we estimate the level-zero parameters A0A_{0}, s0s_{0}, A0reA_{0}^{\mathrm{re}}, and B0B_{0}, and the first-correction prefactors A1A_{1} and A1reA_{1}^{\mathrm{re}}. For ℓ=1,…,L\ell=1,\ldots,L, we then use the propagated surrogates

A^ℓ:=A1​(Δ​tℓΔ​t1)p,A^ℓre:=A1re​(Δ​tℓΔ​t1)p.\widehat{A}_{\ell}:=A_{1}\left(\frac{\Delta t_{\ell}}{\Delta t_{1}}\right)^{p},\hskip 18.49988pt\widehat{A}_{\ell}^{\mathrm{re}}:=A_{1}^{\mathrm{re}}\left(\frac{\Delta t_{\ell}}{\Delta t_{1}}\right)^{p}.

The common algebraic index ss and the common root-exponential rate BB are chosen as described above. Figures 12 and 11 provide numerical evidence that the correction rates are approximately level independent and that both fitted prefactor sequences decay with an exponent close to pp. Thus, the quadrature parameters on the finer correction levels can be constructed without fitting their quadrature errors separately. The propagated prefactors are empirical implementation choices; the algebraic complexity analysis continues to rely on Assumption 11.

4 Numerical Results

In this section, we provide finite-range numerical diagnostics for the assumptions and error estimates introduced in Section 3 and assess the performance of the single-level and multilevel pricing methods developed in Sections 3.2 and 3.3. These diagnostics do not prove the corresponding bounds on the entire Fourier half-line. Section 4.1 studies the convergence of the fractional Adams approximation and of the corresponding fully discrete Fourier integrand. We compare their measured finite-range slopes with the empirical reference rate 1+α1+\alpha discussed in Remark 1; these diagnostics do not assign values to the generic theoretical exponents qq, rTr_{T}, or pp. We also test the sharp price expansion in Assumption 9 and the Richardson estimator of Proposition 3. Section 4.2 examines the choice of the Gauss-Laguerre scaling factor in (37) and the algebraic and root-exponential quadrature error estimates of Section 3.2. For the multilevel method, we additionally examine the regularity of the level differences Δ​gℓ\Delta g_{\ell}, the existence of a common lower bound ss for the smoothness indices sℓs_{\ell} in (62), and the decay of the constants AℓA_{\ell} defined in (61), as assumed in Assumption 11. Finally, Section 4.3 compares the accuracy and computational cost of the single-level and multilevel methods, relates the observed work to the complexity results of Sections 3.2 and 3.3, and compares the multilevel method with the BL2 Markovian approximation in  [7].

Benchmark parameter sets.

We consider European call options throughout the numerical experiments. We use the EuRos and SPY rough Heston parameter sets reported in [12], both originating from calibrations to market implied volatility data, as representative examples of two distinct parameter regimes. The used model parameters are given in Table 1.

Unless stated otherwise, the time-step hierarchy is initialized with Δ​t0=T/32\Delta t_{0}=T/32. The refinement results in Section 4.1 provide numerical evidence, for the tested configurations, that this choice yields stable fractional Adams approximations and that the first levels already exhibit the asymptotic behavior used by the Richardson indicator.

Selection of the damping parameter.

The damping rule proposed in [6] selects RR by solving

R⋆∈arg​minR∈δVsupu∈ℝ|g(u;R,ΘX,ΘP)|=arg​minR∈δV|g(0;R,ΘX,ΘP)|.{R^{\star}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{R\in\delta_{V}}\sup_{u\in\mathbb{R}}|g(u;R,\Theta_{X},\Theta_{P})|=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{R\in\delta_{V}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\left|g(0;R,\Theta_{X},\Theta_{P})\right|}.}

For the rough Heston model, this optimization problem cannot be applied directly because the model admissibility set δX\delta_{X} in Assumption 2, and hence δV=δP∩δX\delta_{V}=\delta_{P}\cap\delta_{X}, is not characterized analytically. Define Moment explosions and critical moments in the rough Heston model are studied in [24, 29]. the right critical log-price moment by

u+​(T):=sup{u>1:𝔼⁡[eu​XT]<∞}.u_{+}(T):=\sup\left\{u>1:\mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{uX_{T}}\right]<\infty\right\}.

For the European call payoff (4), the explicit transform in (5) gives δP=(−∞,−1)\delta_{P}=(-\infty,-1), and full Fourier admissibility requires

R∈(−u+​(T),−1).R\in(-u_{+}(T),-1).

The payoff boundary R=−1R=-1, which corresponds to the pole at ξ=−i\xi=-\mathrm{i}, can be enforced exactly. We therefore take the payoff margin ηP=0.5\eta_{P}=0.5, use R0=−1−ηP=−1.5R_{0}=-1-\eta_{P}=-1.5, and minimize the numerical approximation of |g⁡(0,R,ΘX,ΘP)||g(0;R,\Theta_{X},\Theta_{P})| using L-BFGS-B subject to the one-sided constraint

R≤−1−ηP=−1.5.R\leq-1-\eta_{P}=-1.5.

This constraint guarantees payoff-transform admissibility. However, because no certified value or lower bound for u+​(T)u_{+}(T) is available for the parameter regimes considered, the model-moment boundary R>−u+​(T)R>-u_{+}(T) cannot be enforced. The resulting damping selection is therefore heuristic with respect to model admissibility. Although the numerical Riccati solution is finite at the selected RR, this does not certify model-moment admissibility. The selected damping parameters for every distinct numerical configuration are reported in Table 2 in Appendix I.

The scaling parameter of the Gauss–Laguerre rule is subsequently chosen according to (37).

4.1 Numerical evidence for the time-discretization assumptions

We examine the time-discretization assumptions for the two configurations used in Section 4.3.1: EuRos with T=2T=2, S0=K=1000S_{0}=K=1000, and r=0r=0, and SPY with T=2/365T=2/365, S0=K=1S_{0}=K=1, and r=0r=0. The damping parameter and the default time-step hierarchy are selected as described above. All reported reference quantities use Δ​tref=T/4096\Delta t_{\mathrm{ref}}=T/4096. Unless stated otherwise, the reference Fourier integrals are evaluated using N¯=128\bar{N}=128 Gauss–Laguerre nodes.

We first assess Assumption 3. Since the exact Riccati solution is unavailable, let h¯\bar{h} denote the Adams approximation computed on the reference grid. For numerical validation, we use the reference error

E¯ℓh,w​(u):=max1≤j≤Mℓ⁡tℓ,j1−α​|hℓ,j​(u+i​R)−h¯​(u+i​R,tℓ,j)|.\bar{E}_{\ell}^{\,h,\mathrm{w}}(u):=\max_{1\leq j\leq M_{\ell}}t_{\ell,j}^{1-\alpha}\left|h_{\ell,j}(u+\mathrm{i}R)-\bar{h}(u+\mathrm{i}R,t_{\ell,j})\right|. (72)

Figure 1 provides numerical evidence for Assumption 3 while estimating the numerical rate qq from the decay of E¯ℓh,w​(u)\bar{E}_{\ell}^{\,h,\mathrm{w}}(u) under refinement.

The fitted rates are approximately 1.5951.595–1.5961.596 for EuRos and 1.6681.668–1.7561.756 for SPY, broadly consistent with 1+α=1.621+\alpha=1.62 and 1+α=1.71511+\alpha=1.7151, respectively. As discussed in Remark 1, these results provide numerical evidence for the empirical rate 1+α1+\alpha in the tested configurations, but do not provide a theoretical proof or identify the generic exponent qq. Accordingly, we use 1+α1+\alpha as the numerical rate in the estimators below.

We next assess the time-integration rate rTr_{T} in Assumption 5. For ξ=u+i​R\xi=u+\mathrm{i}R, define the time-integration error

Eℓtime​(ξ):=|∫0T𝒥ξ​(t)​𝑑t−𝒯ℓ​[(𝒥ξ​(tℓ,j))j=0Mℓ]|.E_{\ell}^{\,\mathrm{time}}(\xi):=\left|\int_{0}^{T}\mathcal{J}_{\xi}(t)\,dt-\mathcal{T}_{\ell}\left[\left(\mathcal{J}_{\xi}(t_{\ell,j})\right)_{j=0}^{M_{\ell}}\right]\right|.

The exact function 𝒥ξ\mathcal{J}_{\xi} is unavailable because it depends on the unknown Riccati solution hh. Using h¯\bar{h}, define

The fitted rates are approximately 1.6171.617–1.6221.622 for EuRos and 1.7141.714–1.7171.717 for SPY, which are close to 1+α=1.621+\alpha=1.62 and 1+α=1.71511+\alpha=1.7151, respectively.
