4.2 Scaled Gauss–Laguerre Quadrature and Error Diagnostics

We begin by examining the choice of the scaling parameter σ~\widetilde{\sigma} in (37); see Section 4.2.1. We then turn to the quadrature assumptions underlying the single-level and multilevel analyses of Sections 3.2 and 3.3; see Section 4.2.2. In particular, we consider the algebraic quadrature error estimates and the fitted root-exponential error estimates for the discretized integrands gℓg_{\ell} and the level differences Δ​gℓ\Delta g_{\ell}.

4.2.1 Selection of the scaling parameter

The decay of gℓ​(u)g_{\ell}(u) and Δ​gℓ​(u)\Delta g_{\ell}(u) as u→∞u\to\infty depends on the rough Heston parameters, the maturity TT, and the damping parameter R∈δVR\in\delta_{V}. To illustrate the dependence on maturity, we fix the EuRos parameter set, optimize RR separately for each maturity, and consider T∈{0.1,1,10}T\in\{0.1,1,10\}. Figure 6 shows |g0​(u)|/‖g0‖∞|g_{0}(u)|/\|g_{0}\|_{\infty} and |Δ​g1​(u)|/‖Δ​g1‖∞|\Delta g_{1}(u)|/\|\Delta g_{1}\|_{\infty}, where Δ​g1=g1−g0\Delta g_{1}=g_{1}-g_{0}. The decay is substantially slower for short maturities. This dependence is relevant for the choice of σ~\widetilde{\sigma} because, by (23), the quadrature is applied to g~ℓ​(u)=eσ~​u​gℓ​(u)\widetilde{g}_{\ell}(u)=e^{\widetilde{\sigma}u}g_{\ell}(u). The scale controls the placement of the Laguerre nodes and the constants in the quadrature remainder estimates. Matching it to the estimated Fourier decay can reduce the quadrature error and improve the observed convergence rate. The same principle of adapting the numerical transformation to the decay of the integrand has also been exploited in the quasi Monte Carlo (QMC) and multilevel QMC settings; see [11, 26].

We next compare the quadrature convergence obtained with the standard Gauss–Laguerre rule, corresponding to σ~=1\widetilde{\sigma}=1, with that obtained using the scaling in (37). For each maturity, the damping parameter RR is optimized once and then held fixed across the two scaling choices. The discretization level and all remaining model and payoff parameters are also kept fixed. The quadrature errors are measured relative to a rule with N¯=64\bar{N}=64 quadrature points. Figures 7 and 8 report the quadrature errors for the level-zero integrand g0g_{0} and the first level difference Δ​g1\Delta g_{1}, respectively.

For both g0g_{0} and Δ​g1\Delta g_{1}, the scaling in (37) yields faster convergence at short and long maturities and performs comparably to the standard rule at T=1T=1. We therefore use this scaling in the remaining experiments.

4.2.2 Quadrature error estimates

Throughout this subsection, the fitted values of sℓs_{\ell}, AℓA_{\ell}, and BℓB_{\ell} are numerical estimates obtained from finite-range quadrature errors. They are used to assess consistency with the proposed quadrature models and are not exact values of the theoretical regularity quantities appearing in the assumptions.

The convergence analysis of the Gauss–Laguerre quadrature in Section 3.2 includes the algebraic quadrature error estimate of Theorem 1 and the root-exponential quadrature error estimate of Theorem 2. We first compare the two estimates for g0g_{0} in Figure 9. Over the range of quadrature points considered, the root-exponential estimate provides a closer description of the observed quadrature errors, whereas the algebraic estimate is more conservative. Moreover, the algebraic cover is more sensitive to the range of quadrature orders NN used in its construction. We therefore show separate algebraic covers for the small- and large-NN regimes to assess this sensitivity and illustrate the effect of the selected range. The algebraic estimate, however, permits the explicit optimization and complexity analysis developed in Propositions 4, 8, 6, and 9, including the closed-form expression for the minimum multilevel work in (66). We therefore consider both error estimates in the numerical experiments below.

Transformed integrands. We first examine the conditions used for the transformed integrands g~ℓ\tilde{g}_{\ell}. The algebraic case is covered by Assumption 7 and the uniform bounds in Proposition 6. The root-exponential case is covered by Assumption 8 and the uniform bounds in Proposition 7. We use the EuRos configuration with T=2T=2 and the hierarchy Δ​tℓ=T/(32×2ℓ)\Delta t_{\ell}=T/(32\times 2^{\ell}). At each level, the quadrature error is measured relative to N¯=64\bar{N}=64 quadrature points. Fitting the parameters at every level is performed only to validate the practical approximation described in the theory. The implemented method estimates the level-zero parameters and uses them as surrogates for the parameters at the selected finest level. Figure 10 shows the fitted quadrature-error models for the transformed integrands across the levels considered. The fitted values of the root-exponential parameter satisfy Bℓ≈8.83B_{\ell}\approx 8.83, and a regression of the fitted prefactors gives

Aℓre≈Cre​Δ​tℓ−0.019.A_{\ell}^{\mathrm{re}}\approx C_{\mathrm{re}}\,\Delta t_{\ell}^{-0.019}.

The fitted smoothness indices satisfy sℓ≈8.55s_{\ell}\approx 8.55, while a regression of the corresponding prefactors gives

Aℓ≈Calg​Δ​tℓ 0.001.A_{\ell}\approx C_{\mathrm{alg}}\,\Delta t_{\ell}^{\,0.001}.

Thus, BℓB_{\ell}, sℓs_{\ell}, AℓreA_{\ell}^{\mathrm{re}}, and AℓA_{\ell} depend only weakly on the level over the range considered. These observations are consistent with the bounds in Propositions 6 and 7 being uniform across levels. In particular, the estimated values of sℓs_{\ell} are consistent with taking sSL=8s_{\mathrm{SL}}=8 as the uniform lower bound across these levels.

Level differences. We then examine the level differences Δ​gℓ=gℓ−gℓ−1\Delta g_{\ell}=g_{\ell}-g_{\ell-1}, which enter the multilevel method. Assumptions 10 and 11 require a common lower bound ss for the smoothness indices sℓs_{\ell} and the decay Aℓ=𝒪⁡(Δ​tℓp)A_{\ell}=\mathcal{O}(\Delta t_{\ell}^{p}).

Figures 11 and 12 show the fitted correction models and the scaling of their prefactors.

For the root-exponential fits, the fitted parameters satisfy Bℓ≈8.26B_{\ell}\approx 8.26, while a regression of the fitted prefactors gives the decay rate Δ​tℓ 1.613\Delta t_{\ell}^{\,1.613}. For the algebraic fits, the fitted smoothness indices satisfy sℓ≈7.60s_{\ell}\approx 7.60, while a regression of the fitted prefactors gives the decay rate Δ​tℓ 1.675\Delta t_{\ell}^{\,1.675}.

Both BℓB_{\ell} and sℓs_{\ell} are nearly constant across the levels considered, whereas the fitted prefactors decrease with an exponent close to the observed discretization rate p≈1+α=1.62p\approx 1+\alpha=1.62. The observed algebraic decay Aℓ≈C​Δ​tℓpA_{\ell}\approx C\Delta t_{\ell}^{p} supports Assumption 11. The analogous root-exponential decay Aℓre≈Cre​Δ​tℓpA_{\ell}^{\mathrm{re}}\approx C_{\mathrm{re}}\Delta t_{\ell}^{p} supports the empirical level-scaling rule in Remark 4. Fitting all correction levels here is only diagnostic; the implementation fits A1A_{1} and A1reA_{1}^{\mathrm{re}} and scales them across the finer levels as described there. The values of sℓs_{\ell} are consistent with taking s=7s=7 as a common integer lower bound across these levels. In this configuration, the fitted smoothness indices of the level differences are slightly smaller than those of the transformed integrands, but they remain sufficiently large for the multilevel analysis. The reduction in multilevel work is therefore supported primarily by the decay of the correction prefactors with the level and by the level-dependent allocation of quadrature points.

4.3 Computational Cost Comparison

In this subsection, we first compare the SL and ML methods using the algebraic and root-exponential quadrature error estimates in Section 4.3.1. We then compare the ML method with the BL2 Markovian approximation in Section 4.3.2. To distinguish the computational cost of evaluating an option price from that of selecting the numerical parameters, we report both the pricing CPU time and the total CPU time.

The pricing CPU time is the CPU time required to evaluate the option price after all numerical parameters required by the method have been selected and are reused. For SL, this is the CPU time required for the Gauss–Laguerre quadrature at the selected finest discretization level and with the selected number of quadrature points. For ML, it is the CPU time required for the quadrature of g0g_{0} and the level differences Δ​gℓ\Delta g_{\ell}, using the selected discretization levels and numbers of quadrature points. The total CPU time includes, in addition, the CPU time required for initialization, selection of the damping parameter, computation and fitting of the quadrature error estimates, selection of the discretization level, and selection of the numbers of quadrature points.

4.3.1 Single-Level and Multilevel Methods Comparison

In this section, we compare the single-level and multilevel methods using the algebraic and root-exponential quadrature error estimates. The time discretization and numbers of quadrature points are selected as in Sections 3.2 and 3.3. The figures report the scaled work, CPU time, and relative pricing error with respect to a high-accuracy benchmark price. For the present comparison, we focus on at-the-money options, S0=KS_{0}=K.

Let C0C_{0} be the measured CPU time of one level-zero Riccati evaluation. Using β=2\beta=2, we estimate Cℓ=C0​(Δ​t0/Δ​tℓ)β=C0​ 2β​ℓC_{\ell}=C_{0}(\Delta t_{0}/\Delta t_{\ell})^{\beta}=C_{0}\,2^{\beta\ell}. The reported estimated times are

W^SL=CL​NL,W^ML=C0​N0+∑ℓ=1L(Cℓ−1+Cℓ)​Nℓ.\widehat{W}_{\mathrm{SL}}=C_{L}N_{L},\hskip 18.49988pt\widehat{W}_{\mathrm{ML}}=C_{0}N_{0}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}(C_{\ell-1}+C_{\ell})N_{\ell}.

The relative pricing error is |Vnum−Vref|/|Vref|\lvert V_{\mathrm{num}}-V_{\mathrm{ref}}\rvert/\lvert V_{\mathrm{ref}}\rvert. Thus, a relative target εrel\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}} corresponds to the absolute tolerance ε=εrel​|Vref|\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\lvert V_{\mathrm{ref}}\rvert used in the theory. This reference-based conversion is used only to construct comparable relative-accuracy targets for the numerical benchmark; it is not part of the pricing algorithm, whose input is an absolute tolerance ε>0\varepsilon>0. Since the benchmark price is fixed, this constant change of scale does not alter the complexity exponents. The estimated work is computed from the work proxies in (29) and (58).

The multilevel gain is not specific to this setting and is expected when the integrand has low regularity, since the single-level method then requires many quadrature points on the finest level. Greater regularity of the level differences can further improve the gain, although it is not observed in the present test. The gain depends on the model and numerical setup.

Algebraic quadrature estimate.

We first use the EuRos parameter set in Table 1, with T=2T=2, S0=K=1000S_{0}=K=1000, and r=0r=0. The numerical results in Section 4.1 give the observed convergence rate p≈1+α=1.62p\approx 1+\alpha=1.62 for ‖g−gℓ‖L1​(0,∞)\|g-g_{\ell}\|_{L^{1}(0,\infty)}. The fitted smoothness indices sℓs_{\ell} of the transformed integrands g~ℓ\tilde{g}_{\ell} are approximately 8.558.55 across the levels considered in Figure 10, so we take sSL=8s_{\mathrm{SL}}=8 as the uniform lower bound for the single-level method in Proposition 6. For the multilevel method, the level-zero integrand g0g_{0} is treated separately and has s0=8s_{0}=8. The fitted smoothness index of the correction integrand is approximately 7.687.68, as shown in Figure 12. Consequently, the common correction index in (62) is s=7s=7. The fitted prefactors AℓA_{\ell} for ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1 decrease approximately as Δ​tℓp\Delta t_{\ell}^{p}, consistently with Assumption 11. For the direct fractional Adams implementation described in Section 3.1, the cost exponent is β=2\beta=2.

Here 2​p/β=1.622p/\beta=1.62. Hence s=7>2​p/βs=7>2p/\beta and s0=8≥2​p/βs_{0}=8\geq 2p/\beta, so both conditions required to use the simplified multilevel complexity estimate (69) are satisfied.

Substituting p=1.62p=1.62, β=2\beta=2, and sSL=8s_{\mathrm{SL}}=8 into the single-level complexity estimate (53), and using the multilevel complexity estimate (69), gives

βp+2sSL=1.485andβp=1.235.{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\frac{\beta}{p}+\frac{2}{s_{\mathrm{SL}}}=1.485\hskip 18.49988pt\text{and}\hskip 18.49988pt\frac{\beta}{p}=1.235.}

for the single-level and multilevel methods, respectively.

Figure 13 shows that the computational work required by the ML method increases more slowly than that of the SL method as the relative tolerance is reduced. Both methods satisfy the prescribed relative tolerance, and the dependence of the computational work on the tolerance is consistent with the complexity estimates (53) and (69). More precisely, the fitted exponents displayed in the figure are 1.4581.458 for SL and 1.2371.237 for ML, compared with the predicted exponents 1.4851.485 and 1.2351.235, respectively, over the tested tolerance range.

Root-exponential quadrature estimate.

The separation between SL and ML is generally expected to be less pronounced under the root-exponential estimate because the difference in convergence rates is only logarithmic. We therefore consider a challenging case using the SPY parameter set in Table 1 with the short maturity T=2/365T=2/365, S0=K=1S_{0}=K=1, and r=0r=0. As shown in Figure 6, the integrands decay more slowly as uu increases at short maturities. This makes the single-level quadrature more demanding. The single-level number of quadrature points is selected from (52). For the multilevel method based on the root-exponential quadrature error estimate, the numbers of quadrature points at the different levels are obtained by solving (71). The correction prefactors used in this optimization are constructed with the level-scaling rule of Remark 4.

Figure 14 shows that the multilevel method requires less computational work and has more than ten times lower CPU time at the smallest tested tolerance, while both methods satisfy the prescribed relative tolerance. Section 3.3 does not provide an asymptotic complexity result for the multilevel method based on the root-exponential quadrature error estimate. The comparison in Figure 14 therefore provides numerical evidence that, for this configuration, selecting the number of quadrature points separately at each level reduces both the computational work and the CPU time relative to the single-level method.

4.3.2 Comparison with the BL2 Method

We next compare the multilevel method with the BL2 Markovian approximation of Bayer and Breneis [7]. We restrict the comparison to the multilevel method because Figures 13 and 14 show that it outperforms the single-level method in terms of computational work over the relative tolerances considered. We use the SPY and EuRos parameter sets in Table 1 and consider maturities of two days and one week. For each configuration, the two methods use the same model, payoff, and market parameters. We choose the BL2 approximation because Bayer and Breneis [7] report it as the best-performing among the Markovian approximations considered in their numerical comparison. For each target relative tolerance εrel\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}, we run the reference implementation [13] with internal tolerance εrel/2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}/2 and select the smallest number of factors nBL2∈{1,2,3,4}n_{\mathrm{BL2}}\in\{1,2,3,4\} for which the relative pricing error with respect to the high-accuracy reference price satisfies the prescribed tolerance. The BL2 approximation and selection of nBL2n_{\mathrm{BL2}} are described in Appendix J. This factor-count selection uses VrefV_{\mathrm{ref}} and is therefore a reference-assisted benchmarking procedure, not a production rule for selecting nBL2n_{\mathrm{BL2}}.

Figures 15 and 16 compare the pricing and total CPU times of the multilevel and BL2 methods. For BL2, the pricing CPU time is the CPU time required to evaluate the option price after the number of factors nBL2n_{\mathrm{BL2}} has been selected and the corresponding quadrature nodes and weights have been computed. The total CPU time additionally includes the selection of nBL2n_{\mathrm{BL2}}. Starting from nBL2=1n_{\mathrm{BL2}}=1, the BL2 approximation is constructed and the option price is computed for each candidate number of factors until the resulting relative pricing error satisfies the prescribed tolerance. Each CPU time is the mean of three repetitions, and the selected value of nBL2n_{\mathrm{BL2}} is displayed beside the corresponding BL2 point.

Across the four configurations, ML is substantially faster in total CPU time and is also faster in pricing CPU time except at the tightest tolerance for the one-week SPY case. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed hierarchical framework, particularly in parameter regimes where the Fourier integrand has limited effective regularity and is therefore more demanding to integrate.

5 Conclusion and Future Work

In this work, we introduced a hierarchical Fourier framework for pricing options under the rough Heston model. The main difficulty in this setting comes from the high cost of evaluating the characteristic function, which requires solving a fractional Riccati equation at every quadrature point in the Fourier domain. In the single-level construction, all Fourier nodes are evaluated on the same finest Riccati grid selected for the target accuracy. This can be costly when the required discretization is fine and the quadrature needs many nodes. Both the single- and multilevel constructions use scaled Gauss-Laguerre quadrature, with the scaling chosen to reflect the estimated decay of the Fourier integrand.

For the single-level method, the conditional algebraic analysis gives

WSL(ε)=𝒪(ε−β/p−2/sSL),W_{\mathrm{SL}}(\varepsilon)=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\varepsilon^{-\beta/p-2/s_{\mathrm{SL}}}\right),

whereas, under the multilevel regularity and correction-decay assumptions of Proposition 9, the multilevel work satisfies

WML(ε)=𝒪(ε−2/s0+ε−β/p),W_{\mathrm{ML}}(\varepsilon)=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\varepsilon^{-2/s_{0}}+\varepsilon^{-\beta/p}\right),

and reduces to 𝒪(ε−β/p)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-\beta/p}) when s0≥2​p/βs_{0}\geq 2p/\beta. These are algebraic-cover complexity statements. In the root-exponential regime used in the practical allocation, we do not prove a separate multilevel complexity theorem. The numerical experiments instead show that the level-dependent allocation reduces the number of expensive fine-grid Riccati solves and provides substantial speedups while maintaining the same level of accuracy as the single-level approach. The numerical gains therefore depend on the quadrature regime, model/payoff parameters, hierarchy, and setup cost.

The complexity results are stated for a generic Fourier-integrand convergence rate pp. For the fractional Adams discretization used in the numerical experiments, the results in Section 4.1 indicate the empirical rate p≈1+αp\approx 1+\alpha.

For the four reported SPY and EuRos benchmark configurations, and with the BL2 factor count selected by the reference-assisted procedure described in Section 4.3.2, the present ML implementation has lower total CPU time in the reported measurements.

The framework developed in this work suggests several directions for future work. One natural extension is the use of adaptive time-stepping schemes for the fractional Riccati equation, which may reduce the discretization cost even further. It would also be interesting to study alternative quadrature rules, such as Gauss-Kronrod or double-exponential formulas, and compare their performance with Gauss-Laguerre quadrature in rough volatility settings.

Also understanding the link between the smoothness index sLs_{L} and the roughness parameter α\alpha would give deeper insight into the behavior of the Fourier integrand. Finally, the proposed method can be adapted to other models where the characteristic function is semi-explicit, such as signature volatility models or polynomial Ornstein-Uhlenbeck volatility models.

Δ​tℓ−pG​|1−exp⁡(−Eℓ​(u+i​R))|≤AE​(u)​exp⁡(AE​(u)​Δ​t0pG).\Delta t_{\ell}^{-{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{G}}}\left|1-\exp\!\left(-E_{\ell}(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right)\right|\leq A_{E}(u)\exp\!\left(A_{E}(u)\Delta t_{0}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{G}}}\right). (78)

|Φ⁡(u+i​R)−Φℓ​(u+i​R)|=|Φ⁡(u+i​R)|​|1−exp⁡(−Eℓ​(u+i​R))|≤|Φ⁡(u+i​R)|​Ψ​(u)​Δ​tℓpG.\left|\Phi(u+\mathrm{i}R)-\Phi_{\ell}(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right|=\left|\Phi(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right|\left|1-\exp\!\left(-E_{\ell}(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right)\right|\leq\left|\Phi(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right|\Psi(u)\Delta t_{\ell}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{G}}}. (79)

By the definition of the Fourier integrand, |Re⁡(z)|≤|z||\operatorname{Re}(z)|\leq|z| for every z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C}, and (79),

‖g−gℓ‖L1​(0,∞)\displaystyle\|g-g_{\ell}\|_{L^{1}(0,\infty)} ≤e−r​T2​π​∫0∞|P^​(u+i​R)|​|Φ⁡(u+i​R)−Φℓ​(u+i​R)|​𝑑u\displaystyle\leq\frac{e^{-rT}}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{\infty}\left|\widehat{P}(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right|\left|\Phi(u+\mathrm{i}R)-\Phi_{\ell}(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right|\,du (80)
≤e−r​T2​π​Δ​tℓpG​∫0∞|P^​(u+i​R)|​|Φ⁡(u+i​R)|​Ψ​(u)​du.\displaystyle\leq\frac{e^{-rT}}{2\pi}\Delta t_{\ell}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}p_{G}}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\left|\widehat{P}(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right|\left|\Phi(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right|\Psi(u)\,du.

Proof.

The split constraints in (64) decouple the level-zero variable from the correction variables. At level zero, we solve

and hence

Therefore,

Nℓ⋆=(Aℓcℓ)2/(s+2)(2εquad∑k=1LAk2/(s+2)cks/(s+2))2/s,ℓ=1,…,L.N_{\ell}^{\star}=\left(\frac{A_{\ell}}{c_{\ell}}\right)^{2/(s+2)}\left(\frac{2}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}}}\sum_{k=1}^{L}A_{k}^{2/(s+2)}c_{k}^{s/(s+2)}\right)^{2/s},\hskip 18.49988pt\ell=1,\ldots,L.

Replacing cℓc_{\ell} by Wℓ+Wℓ−1W_{\ell}+W_{\ell-1}, and combining this expression with N0⋆N_{0}^{\star}, proves (65). Substitution into (58) gives (66). ∎

Appendix H Numerical evidence for Conjecture 1

The exact function 𝒟R\mathcal{D}_{R} in (20) cannot be evaluated because the characteristic function Φ\Phi is not available in closed form. We therefore compute a finer-grid approximation Φ¯\bar{\Phi} and, for each tested level ℓ\ell, define the computable normalized function

𝒟¯ℓ,R​(u):=Δ​tℓ−qobs​|P^​(u+i​R)|​|Φ¯​(u+i​R)−Φℓ​(u+i​R)|,u≥0.\overline{\mathcal{D}}_{\ell,R}(u):={\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\Delta t_{\ell}^{-q_{\mathrm{obs}}}}\left|\widehat{P}(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right|\left|\bar{\Phi}(u+\mathrm{i}R)-\Phi_{\ell}(u+\mathrm{i}R)\right|,\hskip 18.49988ptu\geq 0. (89)

Here the overbar indicates that the finer-grid characteristic function is used as the reference quantity. We use the observed rate qobs=1+αq_{\mathrm{obs}}=1+\alpha reported in Section 4.1.

We evaluate (89) for several sufficiently fine levels on a common Fourier grid. On the same grid, we compute the cumulative trapezoidal approximations

I¯ℓ,R​(U):=∫0U𝒟¯ℓ,R​(u)​𝑑u.\overline{I}_{\ell,R}(U):=\int_{0}^{U}\overline{\mathcal{D}}_{\ell,R}(u)\,du. (90)

The observed stabilization of 𝒟¯ℓ,R\overline{\mathcal{D}}_{\ell,R} and the plateau of I¯ℓ,R\overline{I}_{\ell,R} provide numerical support for the decay and integrability required in Conjecture 1. Because the experiment uses a finite Fourier interval, finitely many levels, and the approximation Φ¯\bar{\Phi} in place of Φ\Phi, it does not constitute a proof of integrability on (0,∞)(0,\infty).

Appendix J BL2 Markovian approximation used in the benchmarks

The BL2 method of Bayer and Breneis [7] replaces the fractional kernel in the rough Heston variance equation by a finite sum of exponentials. With H=α−12H=\alpha-\tfrac{1}{2}, it approximates

Kα​(t)=tα−1Γ⁡(α)byKα(n)​(t)=∑j=1nwj​e−xj​t,K_{\alpha}(t)=\frac{t^{\alpha-1}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\hskip 18.49988pt\text{by}\hskip 18.49988ptK_{\alpha}^{(n)}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}e^{-x_{j}t},

where (xj,wj)j=1n(x_{j},w_{j})_{j=1}^{n} are positive nodes and weights. The BL2 rule is the bounded L2​(0,T)L^{2}(0,T) approximation proposed in [7]; the implementation constructs the rules successively, using the optimized (n−1)(n-1)-factor rule to initialize the nn-factor optimization. Hence, nBL2n_{\mathrm{BL2}} is the number of exponential factors, or equivalently the number of kernel-quadrature nodes. It is not the number of Fourier nodes or Riccati time steps.

Introducing U0(j)=0U_{0}^{(j)}=0, the resulting Markovian approximation is

Vt(n):=V0+∑j=1nwj​Ut(j).V_{t}^{(n)}:=V_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}U_{t}^{(j)}.

Together with the asset dynamics in (6), its factors satisfy

d​Ut(j)\displaystyle dU_{t}^{(j)} =[−xjUt(j)+γ(θ−Vt(n))]dt+γνVt(n)dWt2,j=1,…,n,\displaystyle=\left[-x_{j}U_{t}^{(j)}+\gamma\bigl(\theta-V_{t}^{(n)}\bigr)\right]dt+\gamma\nu\sqrt{V_{t}^{(n)}}\,dW_{t}^{2},\hskip 18.49988ptj=1,\ldots,n,

so that the non-Markovian variance equation is replaced by an nn-dimensional Markovian system. In the notation of the reference implementation [13], the parameter conversion is

H=α−12,λ=γ,νBL2=γ​ν,θBL2=γ​θ.H=\alpha-\tfrac{1}{2},\hskip 18.49988pt\lambda=\gamma,\hskip 18.49988pt\nu_{\mathrm{BL2}}=\gamma\nu,\hskip 18.49988pt\theta_{\mathrm{BL2}}=\gamma\theta.

For a prescribed factor count, the implementation calls quadrature_rule with mode="european", which invokes the european_rule construction and returns the kernel nodes and weights. For this fixed rule, the Fourier truncation and the Riccati and Fourier resolutions are then selected adaptively. In our comparison, we precompute one rule for every n∈{1,2,3,4}n\in\{1,2,3,4\}. Given a target relative tolerance εrel\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}, each candidate is priced using the internal tolerance

rel_tolBL2=εrel2.\texttt{rel\_tol}_{\mathrm{BL2}}=\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}}{2}.

This half-tolerance controls the adaptive Fourier and Riccati calculation for the fixed kernel rule; it does not control the finite-factor kernel error. We therefore compute the realized relative pricing error

en:=|VBL2(n)−Vref||Vref|.e_{n}:=\frac{|V_{\mathrm{BL2}}^{(n)}-V_{\mathrm{ref}}|}{|V_{\mathrm{ref}}|}.

We report the smallest factor count satisfying

nBL2:=min⁡{n∈{1,2,3,4}:en≤εrel}.n_{\mathrm{BL2}}:=\min\left\{n\in\{1,2,3,4\}:e_{n}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\right\}. (91)

Thus, we select the minimum number of BL2 kernel-quadrature nodes that attains the target relative error. Since this selection uses VrefV_{\mathrm{ref}}, it is an oracle procedure used only for benchmarking. In our experiments, at most four factors were sufficient to achieve all tested tolerances.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
